title: Cross-correlation of SPT-3G D1 CMB lensing and DES Y3 galaxy lensing
comment: 26 pages, 14 figures
summary: Measurements of the weak lensing of galaxies and of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) provide direct probes of the cosmic matter density field, but the two observables are sensitive to different spatial scales, redshift ranges, and survey systematics. Their cross-correlation thus enables consistency checks of the theoretical model and of potential systematics in either dataset. We present measurements of the cross-correlation between CMB lensing and cosmic shear over $\sim$1,300 deg$^2$ of the sky using the SPT-3G D1 CMB lensing maps and the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES Y3) shear catalogs. For the first time, we measure this cross-correlation at high significance ($\sim 14σ$) when using a polarization-only CMB lensing reconstruction that is expected to be robust against biases induced by extragalactic foregrounds. We test a variety of other CMB lensing estimators that include temperature information and exhibit different tradeoffs between foreground biases and noise, as well as a shear sample that consists of blue, star-forming galaxies and has been shown to be less impacted by galaxy intrinsic alignments. Assuming $Λ$CDM and marginalizing over uncertainties in intrinsic alignments, baryonic feedback, and various nuisance parameters, we obtain a constraint on the amplitude of matter clustering $S_8 \equiv σ_8 \sqrt{Ω_m / 0.3} = 0.833^{+0.047}_{-0.061}$, consistent with both the primary CMB results from Planck and shear-only results from DES Y3. By combining our measurement with Planck, we find mild constraints on the astrophysical processes that impact the cross-correlation. We obtain a constraint on the intrinsic alignment amplitude of the DES sample that is competitive with that from shear-only analyses, and we find a lower limit on the strength of baryonic feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first high-significance (~14σ) measurement of the cross-correlation between CMB lensing (from SPT-3G) and cosmic shear (from DES Y3) over ~1,300 deg², using a polarization-only CMB lensing reconstruction robust against extragalactic foregrounds. The analysis yields a constraint on S₈ = 0.833^{+0.047}_{-0.061}, consistent with both Planck and DES Y3 shear-only results, and provides competitive constraints on intrinsic alignments and baryonic feedback.
AI.motivation: Weak lensing of galaxies (cosmic shear) and CMB lensing probe the same underlying matter density field but are sensitive to different redshift ranges, spatial scales, and systematic effects. Cross-correlating them enables consistency checks of the ΛCDM model and systematics in either dataset, offering a more robust cosmological probe than either alone.
AI.method: The cross-correlation is measured using SPT-3G D1 CMB lensing maps (including polarization-only reconstructions robust against foreground biases) and DES Y3 shear catalogs over ~1,300 deg². Multiple CMB lensing estimators (temperature-inclusive with tradeoffs in foreground bias vs. noise) and a blue, star-forming galaxy shear sample (less impacted by intrinsic alignments) are tested. Constraints are derived marginalizing over intrinsic alignments, baryonic feedback, and nuisance parameters under ΛCDM.
AI.result: A ~14σ detection of the cross-correlation using polarization-only CMB lensing. The S₈ constraint is 0.833^{+0.047}_{-0.061}, consistent with Planck and DES Y3. Combining with Planck yields mild constraints on astrophysical processes, a competitive intrinsic alignment amplitude constraint for the DES sample, and a lower limit on baryonic feedback strength.
AI.conclusion: The cross-correlation between CMB lensing and cosmic shear is robustly detected at high significance, confirming the consistency of ΛCDM across these complementary probes. The results provide competitive constraints on intrinsic alignments and baryonic feedback, and demonstrate the value of joint analysis for mitigating systematics in weak lensing studies.

title: Cutting with precision -- Leveraging Collapse Volumes to generate the next generation of zoom-in initial conditions
comment: submitted to A&A
summary: Astrophysical processes happen across a wide range of scales. This poses a significant challenge from the perspective of modeling these processes. Modern cosmological simulations attempt to maximize the simulation volume to capture the full range of the density power spectrum while simultaneously optimizing spatial resolution for improved modeling of dynamics at galactic scales. Performing zoom-in simulations of galaxy clusters is a way to reconcile computational cost, mass resolution, and large-scale realism in simulations. To study the baryonic evolution of structures it is critical to ensure that the volume of interest is uncontaminated by high-mass particles from outside the zoom-in region. We introduce a new method of constructing stable boundaries for layered zoom-in initial conditions. Applying this method to clusters from the SLOW constrained simulation, we introduce the SLOW cluster zoom-in initial conditions. We select regions using a forward run of a gravity-only version of the parent box. We performed test simulations for a set of 20 regions created from the SLOW constrained simulations containing 30 local clusters. The simulations demonstrate these initial conditions to be stable against deformation and mixing of the boundary region. Consequently, they are uncontaminated to an unprecedented degree, reaching pristine regions of sizes exceeding 6 virial radii. These simulations will provide the basis for the first high-resolution simulations of a large set of directly comparable local galaxy cluster analogues and their environment to date. Their high fidelity in terms of stability and resolution in combination with the accuracy of the underlying local Universe model makes these simulations the first of their kind. They will enable comparisons with state-of-the art observations targeting both cluster properties and ICM physics as well as galaxy evolution in the local Universe.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new method for constructing stable boundary layers in zoom-in initial conditions for cosmological simulations of galaxy clusters. Applied to the SLOW constrained simulation, it produces uncontaminated zoom-in regions exceeding 6 virial radii. These high-fidelity simulations enable direct comparisons with local Universe observations of cluster properties, ICM physics, and galaxy evolution.
AI.motivation: Astrophysical processes span a wide range of scales, making it challenging to model them in simulations. Zoom-in simulations of galaxy clusters are needed to reconcile computational cost, mass resolution, and large-scale realism, but it is critical to ensure the volume of interest is uncontaminated by high-mass particles from outside the zoom-in region.
AI.method: The authors introduce a new method for constructing stable boundaries for layered zoom-in initial conditions. They apply this method to clusters from the SLOW constrained simulation, selecting regions using a forward run of a gravity-only version of the parent box. Test simulations were performed for 20 regions containing 30 local clusters.
AI.result: The initial conditions are stable against deformation and mixing of the boundary region, and are uncontaminated to an unprecedented degree, reaching pristine regions of sizes exceeding 6 virial radii.
AI.conclusion: These simulations provide the basis for the first high-resolution simulations of a large set of directly comparable local galaxy cluster analogues and their environment, enabling comparisons with state-of-the-art observations targeting cluster properties, ICM physics, and galaxy evolution in the local Universe.

title: Lyman-Alpha Forest and its Cross-Correlation with High-Redshift Galaxies in Effective Field Theory at the Field Level
comment: 50 pages, 34 figures, comments welcome
summary: We present a field-level perturbative forward model for the Lyman-alpha (Lya) forest flux decrement. We validate it on two simulation suites: large-volume AbacusSummit N-body simulations with the Lya forest painted onto the dark matter field, and the Sherwood hydrodynamic simulations. Across the redshift range of the simulations (z=2.0-3.2), the 3D and 1D power spectra of the model match the simulated Lya fields at the 1% (5%) level up to k <= 0.3 (1.0) h/Mpc, with similar performance for the cross-correlation with massive dark matter halos. The counts-in-cells statistic shows excellent agreement down to cell radii of 2 Mpc/h. Leveraging cosmic variance cancellation, the model enables precision measurements of Lya bias parameters and robustly detects the full set of quadratic line-of-sight bias operators, consistent with the notion of naturalness in effective field theory (EFT). We quantify the stochasticity of the Lya forest (the analog to the one-halo term), and find it to be white (scale- and orientation-independent) on large scales, matching EFT predictions. We further find that phenomenological flux power spectrum models, based on modulations of the linear-theory power spectrum, fail at the field level even on quasi-linear scales. For the currently observing Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), we generate large-scale clustering mocks of the Lya forest to validate cosmological parameter inference pipelines. Looking ahead to its successor, DESI-II, we produce large-volume mocks of representative samples of Lyman-break galaxies (LBGs) and Lya emitters (LAEs), calibrated on Astrid hydrodynamic simulations and matched to observations at z=3, enabling joint analyses of Lya forest and high-redshift galaxy data.

AI.tldr: A field-level perturbative forward model for the Lyman-alpha forest flux is presented, validated at 1-5% accuracy on simulations, enabling bias measurements, stochasticity quantification, and generation of DESI/DESI-II mocks for joint Lya-galaxy clustering analyses.
AI.motivation: To develop an accurate field-level model for the Lya forest flux that goes beyond phenomenological power spectrum models, enabling precision cosmology with DESI and future surveys by leveraging effective field theory and cosmic variance cancellation.
AI.method: A perturbative forward model based on EFT is constructed and validated against AbacusSummit N-body simulations (with painted Lya forest) and Sherwood hydrodynamic simulations. The model is tested on 3D/1D power spectra, cross-correlations with halos, counts-in-cells statistics, and stochasticity. Mocks are generated for DESI (Lya clustering) and DESI-II (joint Lya, LBG, LAE samples calibrated on Astrid simulations).
AI.result: 3D and 1D power spectra match simulations at 1% up to k≤0.3 h/Mpc and 5% up to k≤1.0 h/Mpc. Cross-correlation with halos shows similar performance. Counts-in-cells agrees down to 2 Mpc/h. The full set of quadratic line-of-sight bias operators is robustly detected. Lya stochasticity is found to be white (scale- and orientation-independent) on large scales. Phenomenological flux power spectrum models fail at field level even on quasi-linear scales.
AI.conclusion: The EFT-based forward model is validated as highly accurate for Lya forest clustering, enables natural bias parameter measurements, and produces realistic mocks for DESI and DESI-II, supporting joint analyses of Lya forest and high-redshift galaxies (LBGs/LAEs).

title: First full-shape joint analysis of the two- and three-point correlation functions on real data: $Λ$CDM cosmological constraints from BOSS DR12
comment: 19 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to A&A
summary: The three-point correlation function (3PCF) encodes cosmological information beyond the two-point correlation function (2PCF), yet a full-shape joint analysis in redshift space using real data has so far been lacking. We present the first full-shape cosmological constraints from a joint analysis of 2PCF and 3PCF in redshift space, using BOSS DR12 data, extending to real data, including Alcock--Paczyński and redsfhit space distortions, the full-shape configuration-space framework validated in real space for the first time by Euclid Collaboration: Guidi et al (2026). We model both statistics adopting the velocity difference generating function (VDG) framework, incorporating non-perturbative Fingers-of-God damping, a complete Eulerian galaxy bias expansion, and infrared resummation. Fast and accurate theoretical predictions are obtained using dedicated emulators, which enable a full-shape likelihood analysis of the 3PCF and its combination with the 2PCF, varying the cosmological parameters $10^9 A_s, ω_{\rm cdm}$ and $h$, while the baryon fraction density $ω_{b}$ is fixed to its fiducial value. The covariance matrix is estimated from 2048 MultiDark-Patchy mocks, and an optimal data-vector compression ensures a stable covariance inversion. The perturbative model is validated against goodness-of-fit tests across different scales, and provides a good description of the joint data vector down to $r_{\rm min}^{\rm 3PCF} \sim 60\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$. We find that the joint 2PCF+3PCF analysis yields significant improvements over the 2PCF-only baseline, with gains of approximately 29\%, 10\%, and 24\% on $σ(h)$, $σ(ω_{\rm cdm})$, and $σ(A_s)$, respectively. The improvements mainly arise from the additional BAO cosmological information encoded in the 3PCF triangle configurations.

AI.tldr: First full-shape joint 2PCF+3PCF cosmological constraints in redshift space using BOSS DR12 data, showing ~10-29% parameter improvements over 2PCF alone.
AI.motivation: The 3PCF contains cosmological information beyond the 2PCF, but a full-shape joint analysis in redshift space with real data had not been performed until this work.
AI.method: Joint analysis of 2PCF and 3PCF in redshift space using the VDG framework with non-perturbative FoG damping, Eulerian galaxy bias expansion, IR resummation, and emulators. Covariance from 2048 MultiDark-Patchy mocks with optimal data compression. Varying $10^9 A_s$, $\omega_{\rm cdm}$, $h$ while fixing $\omega_b$.
AI.result: Joint 2PCF+3PCF improves constraints by ~29% on $\sigma(h)$, 10% on $\sigma(\omega_{\rm cdm})$, and 24% on $\sigma(A_s)$ over 2PCF-only. Model valid down to $r_{\min}^{\rm 3PCF} \sim 60\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$.
AI.conclusion: The 3PCF adds significant cosmological information (mainly from BAO in triangle configurations), enabling tighter constraints in full-shape redshift-space analysis.

title: Dark Matter in Draco and Boötes I: Hints of a Core in an Ultra-Faint Dwarf from Simulation-Based Inference
comment: 33 + 8 pages, 13 + 8 figures, 5 tables, submitted to MNRAS
summary: The density profiles of dwarf spheroidal galaxies are among the most sensitive probes of dark matter physics, yet extracting them from noisy stellar kinematics remains a fundamental obstacle. We present GraphNPE, a simulation-based inference method for dynamical mass modeling that incorporates measurement uncertainties and spectroscopic selection functions in the forward model. Using mock data, we show that methods relying solely on line-of-sight velocity dispersion are biased toward cuspy density profiles, even in the absence of the mass-anisotropy degeneracy. By accessing higher-order velocity moments, particularly line-of-sight kurtosis, GraphNPE breaks key degeneracies and recovers density profiles with substantially less bias. We apply GraphNPE to Draco and Boötes I using MMT/Hectochelle and DESI for Draco, and the S5 survey for Boötes I. For each, we report density profiles and dark matter $J$- and $D$-factors. For Draco, GraphNPE yields consistent results across datasets, marginally preferring a cuspy inner profile ($ρ_{150} \sim 1.6-1.9 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{M}_\odot\,\mathrm{kpc}^{-3}$) in agreement with literature. On DESI, however, second-order Jeans modeling fits the dispersion but fails to reproduce the kurtosis, demonstrating higher-order moments are essential. For Boötes I, limited statistical power prevents definitive determination of the inner slope. GraphNPE recovers $ρ_{150} = 0.36^{+0.15}_{-0.11} \times 10^8\,\mathrm{M}_\odot\,\mathrm{kpc}^{-3}$, significantly lower than literature and consistent with a cored inner profile. This places Boötes I among the lowest density dwarfs at comparable stellar masses.

AI.tldr: GraphNPE is a simulation-based inference method for dynamical mass modeling of dwarf spheroidal galaxies that uses higher-order velocity moments (kurtosis) to break degeneracies and reduce bias in density profile recovery. Applied to Draco, it finds cuspy profiles consistent across datasets; applied to Boötes I, it finds significantly lower densities consistent with a core, making it among the lowest density dwarfs.
AI.motivation: Density profiles of dwarf spheroidal galaxies are sensitive probes of dark matter physics, but extracting them from noisy stellar kinematics is fundamentally difficult. Existing methods relying solely on line-of-sight velocity dispersion are biased toward cuspy profiles, and the mass-anisotropy degeneracy further complicates inference.
AI.method: GraphNPE (Graph Neural Posterior Estimation) is a simulation-based inference approach that forward-models measurement uncertainties and spectroscopic selection functions. It accesses higher-order velocity moments (line-of-sight kurtosis) beyond the standard second-order dispersion to break the mass-anisotropy degeneracy and reduce bias.
AI.result: Mock data show dispersion-only methods are biased toward cuspy profiles. For Draco, GraphNPE finds consistent cuspy inner profiles (ρ₁₅₀ ~ 1.6-1.9 × 10⁸ M⊙ kpc⁻³) across MMT/Hectochelle and DESI datasets, but DESI second-order Jeans modeling fails to reproduce the kurtosis. For Boötes I, GraphNPE recovers ρ₁₅₀ = 0.36^{+0.15}_{-0.11} × 10⁸ M⊙ kpc⁻³, consistent with a core and significantly lower than literature.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order velocity moments are essential for unbiased dark matter density profile inference. GraphNPE successfully breaks key degeneracies and reveals significant differences in density profiles: Draco is cuspy, while Boötes I is among the lowest density dwarfs and consistent with cored dark matter.

title: Overview of 21cm Experiments at high redshift with SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Trott01
summary: We provide an overview of the eight SKAO Science Book chapters that motivate the Epoch of Reionisation and Cosmic Dawn experiments with SKA-Low. We describe the individual SKA-Low experiments and expected sensitivity - power spectrum, tomography, 21-cm forest, cross-correlations, building on the broad observational plan laid out in the 2015 SKA Science Book. AI.tldr: This paper provides an overview of eight SKAO Science Book chapters motivating the Epoch of Reionisation and Cosmic Dawn experiments with SKA-Low, describing the individual experiments, expected sensitivity, and critical telescope features for EoR/CD science.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the scientific motivation and observational plan for studying the Epoch of Reionisation and Cosmic Dawn using the SKA-Low telescope, building on the 2015 SKA Science Book.
AI.method: Review of eight SKAO Science Book chapters describing SKA-Low experiments including power spectrum measurements, tomography, 21-cm forest, and cross-correlations, along with analysis of telescope features such as beam apodization, substations, and multi-beaming.
AI.result: Describes the expected sensitivity and observational capabilities of SKA-Low for EoR/CD science, including the critical telescope features needed for success.

title: Latent thermal instability
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. To be submitted, comments are welcome
summary: Multiscale temperature fluctuations are abundant in the intracluster medium (ICM) outside of galaxy cluster cores ($\sim 100~{\rm kpc}$). Their origin is often attributed to turbulent stirring by subhalos or accreting baryons crossing the virial radius. However, their apparent resistance to mixing and thermal conduction in a collisional medium has not been explained. We propose a new mechanism by which steady-state temperature fluctuations can form and persist outside the cluster core. Local thermal instability, or Field instability, is used to explain filamentary condensates in cluster cores but is usually dismissed outside them because thermal conduction should suppress instability. In weakly collisional or collisionless plasmas, however, thermal conduction can be anomalously suppressed by heat-flux-driven plasma instabilities triggered in presence of a local magnetic field, leading to two effects: (i) condensates form in a new parameter regime that overlaps with conditions outside the core, and (ii) condensates reach a steady state as in the hydrodynamic limit. This extends the regime of instability-driven fluctuations to over $\gtrsim50\%$ (depending on hot plasma temperature) of the cluster. We use one-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of condensates to test our analytical ideas.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that local thermal (Field) instability, enabled by anomalous suppression of thermal conduction via heat-flux-driven plasma instabilities in weakly collisional/collisionless plasmas, can explain persistent multiscale temperature fluctuations outside galaxy cluster cores, extending the instability regime to over 50% of the cluster volume.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin and persistence of multiscale temperature fluctuations in the intracluster medium (ICM) outside cluster cores (~100 kpc), which are commonly observed but not well understood, particularly their resistance to mixing and thermal conduction in a collisional medium.
AI.method: The authors propose a theoretical mechanism where heat-flux-driven plasma instabilities anomalously suppress thermal conduction in weakly collisional/collisionless plasmas, allowing local thermal (Field) instability to operate outside cluster cores. They use 1D hydrodynamic simulations of condensates to test their analytical predictions.
AI.result: The proposed mechanism extends the regime of instability-driven temperature fluctuations to over 50% of the cluster (depending on hot plasma temperature). Condensates form in a new parameter regime overlapping with conditions outside the core and can reach a steady state, similar to the hydrodynamic limit.
AI.conclusion: Local thermal instability, previously dismissed outside cluster cores due to thermal conduction, can persist there if conduction is anomalously suppressed by plasma instabilities. This provides a viable explanation for observed persistent temperature fluctuations in the ICM beyond the core region.

title: The SKA View of the Sunyaev-Zeldovich Effect from Massive Cosmic Halos
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Perrott01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The thermal intracluster medium (ICM) can be observed via its interaction with Cosmic Microwave Background photons, known as the Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) effect. This effect produces an observable signal at radio to sub-mm wavelengths which probes the pressure of the ICM. The SKA will be sensitive to the thermal SZ effect in its highest frequency band, 5b. In this Chapter, we show that the SKA will provide a high-resolution, high-sensitivity view of the thermal SZ effect, allowing detailed observations of pressure substructures in clusters while retaining sensitivity to the large-scale global ICM emission.

AI.tldr: The paper describes how the SKA telescope in its highest frequency band (5b) will observe the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect to study the intracluster medium, providing high-resolution and high-sensitivity measurements of pressure substructures in galaxy clusters while maintaining sensitivity to large-scale emission.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the capability of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) for observing the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, enabling detailed studies of pressure substructures in the intracluster medium of galaxy clusters.
AI.method: Utilizing the SKA's highest frequency band (5b) to observe the thermal SZ effect, which probes ICM pressure via the interaction between the ICM and Cosmic Microwave Background photons.
AI.result: The SKA will provide high-resolution, high-sensitivity observations of the thermal SZ effect, allowing detection of pressure substructures in clusters while retaining sensitivity to large-scale global ICM emission.
AI.conclusion: The SKA is a powerful instrument for thermal SZ effect observations, bridging the gap between high-resolution substructure analysis and large-scale ICM studies.

title: Cluster vs Field: Clear Evidence for a Morphology-Density Relation in All Environments at $z\sim1.6$
comment: 23 pages, 13 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We explore the relationship between galaxy structure, stellar mass, and local galaxy density in three SpARCS clusters at $z\sim1.6$ and compare with field galaxies from the 3D-HST survey. Our cluster and field data include: 1) unprecedented multiband photometry, allowing for accurate stellar mass estimates; 2) extensive slit and grism spectroscopy targeting both star-forming and quiescent galaxies, allowing for high-accuracy local density measurements; and 3) deep imaging in F160W, allowing for accurate rest-frame optical morphologies. Using Sérsic index measured in rest-frame R-band, we classify galaxies as disk-like, bulge-like, and intermediate. Our sample includes 111 cluster galaxies and 458 field galaxies with reliable Sérsic measurements. We find that a morphology-density relation is already in-place in both cluster and field galaxies at $z\sim1.6$, such that as local density increases, the fraction of bulge-like galaxies increases and disk-like galaxies decreases. Both samples show similar positive trends between median Sérsic index and local density. Additionally, we find a general positive relationship between Sérsic index and stellar mass. The majority of galaxies remain disk-like until reaching stellar masses above $10^{10.25} M_\odot$ in the cluster or $10^{10.8} M_\odot$ in the field, however, we cannot conclude whether the differences in stellar mass trends are significant. Overall, our results show clear morphology-density and morphology-mass relations in place at $z\sim1.6$ and oppose the idea that cluster-specific processes are solely responsible the morphology-density relation. Our data further suggest that the morphology-density relation may be independent of global environment at this epoch.

AI.tldr: This study examines galaxy morphology, stellar mass, and local density in three SpARCS clusters at z~1.6 compared to field galaxies from 3D-HST. Using Sérsic index classifications, the authors find that a morphology-density relation exists at z~1.6 in both cluster and field environments, with bulge-like galaxies increasing and disk-like galaxies decreasing as local density rises. They also find a positive relationship between Sérsic index and stellar mass, with disk-like galaxies persisting to higher masses in the field. Results suggest the morphology-density relation is already in place at this epoch and may be independent of global environment.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the morphology-density relation exists at z~1.6 and whether cluster-specific processes are necessary to drive it, or if it is already in place across all environments at this early epoch.
AI.method: Analysis of 111 cluster and 458 field galaxies at z~1.6 using multiband photometry for stellar masses, slit/grism spectroscopy for local density measurements, and deep F160W imaging for rest-frame optical morphologies (Sérsic index classification into disk-like, bulge-like, intermediate).
AI.result: A morphology-density relation exists at z~1.6: bulge-like fraction increases and disk-like fraction decreases with higher local density in both cluster and field. Positive correlation between Sérsic index and stellar mass is found. Most galaxies remain disk-like below ~10^10.25 M⊙ (cluster) or ~10^10.8 M⊙ (field).
AI.conclusion: The morphology-density relation is already in place at z~1.6 and does not require cluster-specific processes to explain it. The relation may be independent of global environment at this epoch, suggesting environmental quenching mechanisms are universal.

title: Probing inflationary particle production with the CMB power spectrum
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures
summary: Particle production is common to many microphysical models of inflation and can imprint observable features in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies. We consider a scenario in which the inflaton couples to an extremely massive field ($m_χ\gtrsim \mathcal{O}(100 H_I)$, where $H_I$ is the inflationary Hubble scale). In this model, particle production happens in a burst at a characteristic conformal time, $η_*$, which sources localized features in the CMB. In this paper, we compute the full temperature and polarization two-point functions for this model. We then search for these features in CMB power spectrum data from Planck and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), with the latter allowing access to features on smaller angular scales. In the joint analysis of Planck and ACT data, we find a mild $\sim 2 σ$ hint for a signal induced by this inflationary model on scales $3 \,\, \text{Mpc}\leqη_*\leq 10 \,\, \text{Mpc}$, though this hint is not present at a statistically significant level in either dataset when analyzed individually. Using a Fisher forecast, we find that these features should be observable at the $3-5σ$ level for a Simons Observatory-like experiment, if they are indeed real. We also compare our power-spectrum-based constraints to previous matched-filter-based bounds on this model. For sufficiently light particles ($m_χ\lesssim 200 H_I$), the power spectrum yields tighter constraints by more than an order of magnitude, but in the higher-mass regime where particle production is rare, the matched-filter approach provides stronger bounds.

AI.tldr: This paper studies inflationary particle production from a massive field (m_χ ≳ 100 H_I), computes the full CMB temperature and polarization two-point functions, and searches for these features in Planck and ACT data. A mild ~2σ hint is found on scales 3-10 Mpc in the joint analysis, but not individually. Fisher forecasts suggest Simons Observatory could detect these at 3-5σ. Power spectrum constraints outperform matched-filter bounds for light particles (m_χ ≲ 200 H_I), while matched-filter is stronger for rare, higher-mass particle production.
AI.motivation: To search for observable signatures in the CMB from particle production during inflation, specifically from inflaton coupling to an extremely massive field, and to determine whether current or future experiments can detect these features.
AI.method: The authors compute the full temperature and polarization CMB two-point functions for the model, then perform a joint likelihood analysis using Planck and ACT data. Fisher forecasts are used to assess detectability with future experiments like Simons Observatory. Constraints are also compared to matched-filter-based bounds.
AI.result: A mild ~2σ hint for a signal is found on scales 3 Mpc ≤ η_* ≤ 10 Mpc in joint Planck+ACT analysis, but not significant individually. Forecasts indicate Simons Observatory could achieve 3-5σ detection if signal is real. Power spectrum gives tighter constraints than matched-filter for m_χ ≲ 200 H_I, while matched-filter is better for higher masses.
AI.conclusion: The inflationary particle production model is not significantly detected in current data, but future experiments may confirm or rule it out. The optimal analysis method depends on the mass regime of the produced particle.

title: Quantifying the inside-out formation of disk galaxies at $1.5 \le z \le 3.0$
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: We examine the properties of galaxies at $1.5\le z\le3.0$ in the Extended Groth Strip (EGS) field to explore inside-out disk growth. We take advantage of the high-resolution James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) imaging and imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) to measure rest-frame optical and rest-frame UV half-light radii of the galaxies at comparable spatial resolution. We also examine the relation between structural properties and star formation rates, mass, and dust attenuation. While previous studies have inferred inside-out disk formation via the comparison of rest-optical and rest-UV radii using HST images, this study advances this knowledge by using the unprecedented resolution of JWST. We find evidence of inside-out disk formation from, on average, larger UV sizes than optical for galaxies across all redshifts. While previous studies suggested that this could be accounted for due to dust, we find that measurements with the improved resolution of the JWST support this size difference, after accounting for dust attenuation. We also observe that majority of galaxies with clumpy morphologies ($n < 0.5$) exhibit larger UV sizes than rest-optical because the star formation is distributed in multiple star forming clumps or mergers. We observe correlations in both the optical and UV for the size-mass relation, which are consistent with previous results but we find lower values for the slope of the power-law relation of the rest-optical fit, based on robust measurements from JWST images compared to the low resolution HST images used in previous studies.

AI.tldr: This study uses high-resolution JWST (and HST) imaging to analyze galaxies at z=1.5-3.0 in the EGS field, finding evidence for inside-out disk growth from larger UV half-light radii compared to optical, robust against dust effects, with clumpy morphologies (n<0.5) showing similar size differences, and deriving updated lower slope values for the rest-optical size-mass relation.
AI.motivation: To advance the understanding of inside-out disk formation in high-redshift galaxies by leveraging the unprecedented resolution of JWST to measure rest-frame optical and UV half-light radii, overcoming limitations of previous HST-based studies.
AI.method: Analysis of galaxies at 1.5≤z≤3.0 in the Extended Groth Strip (EGS) using high-resolution JWST and HST imaging; measurement of rest-frame optical and UV half-light radii at comparable spatial resolution; examination of structural properties, star formation rates, mass, and dust attenuation.
AI.result: Larger UV sizes than optical sizes across all redshifts support inside-out disk formation; the size difference persists after accounting for dust attenuation with JWST's improved resolution; galaxies with clumpy morphologies (n<0.5) show larger UV sizes due to distributed star formation; the size-mass relation slope for rest-optical is lower than previous HST-based estimates.
AI.conclusion: JWST observations confirm inside-out disk growth at z=1.5-3.0, with the UV-optical size difference robust against dust effects, and provide more accurate measurements of structural scaling relations.

title: Distance-Ladder Measurements of the Hubble Constant: Recent Progress, Systematics, and Prospects
comment: Review article; accepted for publication in Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics; 38 pages, 6 figures; comments welcome
summary: The Hubble constant, \(H_0\), links the nearby distance scale to the present cosmic expansion rate. Local distance-ladder measurements now reach percent-level precision and remain more than \(5σ\) higher than the value inferred from cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations in base-\(Λ\)CDM, making the reliability of the local ladder a central issue in the Hubble tension. We describe the ladder as a covariance network connecting level-0 geometric anchors, level-1 stellar distance indicators, and level-2 Hubble-flow probes. The Cepheid--Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) route remains the most precise single local ladder, but independent indicators including the tip of the red giant branch (TRGB), J-region asymptotic giant branch (JAGB) stars, Mira variables, surface-brightness fluctuations (SBF), the Tully--Fisher relation, and Type II supernovae (SNe II) now test shared and method-specific systematics. In a compact seven-route covariance summary, combining the Cepheid--SN Ia route with three level-1 alternatives (TRGB, JAGB, and Mira) and three level-2 alternatives (SBF, Tully--Fisher, and SNe II) gives \(H_0=73.30\pm0.92~{\rm km~s^{-1}~Mpc^{-1}}\), still \(5.6σ\) above Planck base-\(Λ\)CDM. JWST has already tested Cepheid crowding and is making independent TRGB-based \(H_0\) measurements increasingly feasible. Over the next five years, a reliable one-percent local \(H_0\) requires larger calibrator samples, cross-validated level-1 zero points, explicit covariance propagation, and AI-assisted, reproducible, pre-specified selection criteria for distance-indicator measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the Hubble constant tension by modeling the distance ladder as a covariance network across three levels (geometric anchors, stellar indicators, and Hubble-flow probes). A seven-route combination yields H₀=73.30±0.92 km/s/Mpc, 5.6σ above Planck base-ΛCDM. Future progress requires larger samples, cross-validated zero points, explicit covariance, and AI-assisted reproducible selection criteria.
AI.motivation: The Hubble tension (5σ+ discrepancy between local distance-ladder H₀ measurements and CMB-inferred values in base-ΛCDM) calls into question the reliability of the local distance ladder, motivating a systematic assessment of its covariance structure and cross-validation across multiple independent distance indicators.
AI.method: The distance ladder is formalized as a three-level covariance network (level-0: geometric anchors, level-1: stellar distance indicators like Cepheids/TRGB/JAGB/Mira, level-2: Hubble-flow probes like SBF/Tully-Fisher/SNe II). A compact seven-route covariance summary combines the Cepheid-SN Ia route with three level-1 and three level-2 alternatives.
AI.result: The combined seven-route analysis yields H₀=73.30±0.92 km/s/Mpc, maintaining a 5.6σ tension with Planck base-ΛCDM values. JWST has tested Cepheid crowding and enables independent TRGB-based measurements.
AI.conclusion: Achieving a reliable 1% local H₀ within five years requires larger calibrator samples, cross-validated level-1 zero points, explicit covariance propagation, and AI-assisted, reproducible, pre-specified selection criteria for distance-indicator measurements.

title: The 10-15 GHz radio continuum survey of the Galactic Plane with SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:26.06.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Traficante01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Star formation emerges from the complex interplay between gravity, turbulence, magnetic fields, and stellar feedback, all of which vary across spatial scales and Galactic environments. Over the past decades, extensive multiwavelength surveys of the Galactic Plane have progressively unveiled this complexity. Far-infrared and sub-millimetre surveys have identified and characterized tens of thousands of star-forming regions, revealing their mass, temperature, and evolutionary stage. Complementary molecular-line surveys, spanning several CO transitions and isotopologues, have mapped the gas kinematics from giant molecular clouds down to sub-parsec structures. The advent of interferometers such as ALMA has revolutionized this field, enabling systematic studies of gas dynamics, fragmentation, and collapse in dense clumps at scales of a few thousand astronomical units. At the same time, mid-infrared and radio surveys at frequencies 0.8 <= nu <= 5 GHz have traced ionised gas associated with the earliest and latest phases of massive-star evolution, including thermal radio jets, hypercompact and ultracompact HII regions, supernova remnants, planetary nebulae, and evolved massive stars. Yet, a uniform, Galaxy-wide census of ionised structures and feedback processes remains elusive. A transformational leap forward requires a sensitive, high-resolution radio survey of the Galactic Plane at 10-15 GHz, capable of resolving physical scales smaller than 0.05 pc at distances up to 20 kpc. This is precisely the goal of the SKA-Mid Galactic Plane survey, which will, with its unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and mapping speed, provide the first panoptic view of ionised gas and stellar feedback across the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews multiwavelength surveys of Galactic star formation and argues that a transformational leap requires a sensitive, high-resolution SKA-Mid radio survey at 10–15 GHz to provide the first panoptic view of ionised gas and stellar feedback across the Milky Way.
AI.motivation: Despite extensive multiwavelength surveys (far-infrared, sub-mm, molecular-line, ALMA, mid-infrared, radio), a uniform Galaxy-wide census of ionised structures and feedback processes remains elusive, motivating the need for a transformative radio survey.
AI.method: The paper synthesizes results from past and ongoing surveys across the electromagnetic spectrum (far-IR, sub-mm, CO lines, ALMA, mid-IR, radio at 0.8–5 GHz) and identifies key observational gaps, then proposes the SKA-Mid Galactic Plane survey at 10–15 GHz as the next methodological step.
AI.result: Past surveys have identified tens of thousands of star-forming regions, mapped gas kinematics from cloud to sub-parsec scales, and traced ionised gas in various massive-star evolutionary phases, but lack uniform Galaxy-wide coverage of ionised structures and feedback.
AI.conclusion: The SKA-Mid Galactic Plane survey at 10–15 GHz, with its unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution (sub-0.05 pc at 20 kpc), and mapping speed, will provide the first panoptic view of ionised gas and stellar feedback across the Milky Way, representing a transformational leap forward.

title: Quintom Model Perturbations
comment: 12 pages, 12 figures, comments welcome
summary: We build upon the work of Goh and Taylor 2025, in which we proposed a two scalar field quintom framework capable of naturally realising a phantom-to-quintessence transition in the dark energy equation of state. In this work, we derive the linear perturbation equations of our model and investigate its implications for large scale structure formation. We show that the quintom model is able to reproduce the phenomenological features of a w0waCDM cosmology with phantom-to-quintessence crossing, including suppressions in the matter power spectrum and enhancements to the late-time Integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect. We then perform a Bayesian analysis of the quintom framework with BAO, CMB and Type 1a supernovae data, finding that it is mildly favoured over the standard w0waCDM parametrisation, while successfully reproducing physical trends observed in the data. We further examine the parameter degeneracies inherent to the model and discuss prospective observational strategies for distinguishing quintom cosmologies from conventional dynamical dark energy models given current and future data precision.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a two-scalar-field quintom dark energy model by deriving its linear perturbation equations, showing it can reproduce w0waCDM phenomenology (matter power spectrum suppressions, enhanced ISW effect), and performing Bayesian analysis with BAO, CMB, and SNIa data, finding it mildly favored over standard parametrizations while discussing parameter degeneracies and observational strategies.
AI.motivation: To provide a physical field-theoretic framework (quintom) that can naturally realize a phantom-to-quintessence crossing in dark energy equation of state, going beyond phenomenological parametrizations like w0waCDM, and to test its viability against observational data.
AI.method: Derivation of linear perturbation equations for the two-scalar-field quintom model; comparison of predicted matter power spectrum and ISW effect with w0waCDM; Bayesian analysis using BAO, CMB, and Type Ia supernova data; examination of parameter degeneracies.
AI.result: The quintom model reproduces phenomenological features of w0waCDM with phantom-to-quintessence crossing (suppressed matter power spectrum, enhanced late-time ISW effect). Bayesian analysis shows it is mildly favored over standard w0waCDM and successfully reproduces physical trends in observational data.
AI.conclusion: The quintom framework offers a viable physical mechanism for phantom-to-quintessence transitions in dark energy, is mildly preferred by current data, and warrants further observational discrimination strategies.

title: Wind Acceleration as a Driver of Detached Blueshifted Absorption in Quasar Disk Winds
comment: 1 Table, 4 Figures
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) unification models often emphasize the viewing angle, $i$, but $i$ alone does not determine quasar properties. This is crucial for quasar outflows: UV absorption in Extremely High Velocity Outflow (EHVO) quasars can reach blueshifted velocities of $\sim0.2~c$. In disk-wind models, both $i$ and internal wind structure shape the emergent spectrum. We test their interplay using biconical quasar disk-wind models with different acceleration lengths, $R_v$, and generate synthetic spectra over a range of $i$. We use Monte Carlo radiative transfer to account for finite continuum sources, wind attenuation, scattering, reprocessing, and emission. Changing $R_v$ greatly alters the ionization structure, continuum shape, and absorption-line profiles. At intermediate viewing angles, sightlines pass through the fastest wind. Even there, highly detached and blueshifted \CIV\ absorption like that observed in EHVO quasars appears only in models with small $R_v$. In these models, the gas reaches high velocity before attaining the ionization and density conditions favorable for \CIV. Models with larger $R_v$ instead produce broader, less detached troughs, even when the terminal velocity is very high. Thus, highly detached and blueshifted absorption requires both a high terminal velocity and small $R_v$, making such features diagnostics of disk-wind acceleration and structure. EHVO quasars provide a clear example, but the same principle applies more broadly to highly detached and blueshifted absorption in quasar outflows. Our results support an extended disk-wind view of AGN unification: $i$ selects the observed wind region, while $R_v$ shapes the emergent spectrum and absorption morphology.

AI.tldr: Quasar disk-wind models show that highly detached and blueshifted UV absorption (e.g., in EHVO quasars) requires both high terminal velocity and small acceleration length ($R_v$); viewing angle alone is insufficient to explain outflow properties, supporting an extended AGN unification where $R_v$ shapes the spectrum alongside inclination.
AI.motivation: AGN unification models typically focus on viewing angle ($i$) but fail to explain observed diversity in quasar outflow properties, especially extremely high velocity outflows (EHVOs) with blueshifted absorption up to ~0.2c. The interplay between viewing angle and internal wind structure (acceleration length $R_v$) needs investigation.
AI.method: Biconical quasar disk-wind models with varying acceleration lengths ($R_v$) were constructed. Synthetic spectra were generated over a range of viewing angles using Monte Carlo radiative transfer, accounting for finite continuum sources, wind attenuation, scattering, reprocessing, and emission.
AI.result: Changing $R_v$ significantly alters ionization structure, continuum shape, and absorption-line profiles. Highly detached and blueshifted CIV absorption (as seen in EHVO quasars) only appears in models with small $R_v$, where gas reaches high velocity before favorable ionization/density conditions for CIV. Larger $R_v$ models produce broader, less detached troughs even at very high terminal velocities.
AI.conclusion: Highly detached and blueshifted absorption requires both high terminal velocity and small $R_v$, making such features diagnostics of disk-wind acceleration and structure. Results support an extended disk-wind AGN unification: $i$ selects the observed wind region, while $R_v$ shapes the emergent spectrum and absorption morphology.

title: Spherical Collapse and Halo Formation in a Cosmology with Decaying Dark Matter and a Semi-Cosmographic Dark Energy
comment: Submitted.15 Pages, 7 figures
summary: We investigate nonlinear structure formation in a cosmological model combining one-body decaying dark matter (DDM) with a semi-cosmographic reconstruction of dark energy. In this scenario, a nonrelativistic dark-matter component decays into relativistic dark radiation with decay rate $Γ=τ_{\rm ddm}^{-1}$, while the dark-energy sector is reconstructed directly from the expansion history rather than being fixed to a cosmological constant. Using DESI DR1 BAO and compressed ShapeFit measurements, we constrain the background evolution and propagate the resulting posterior into the nonlinear regime through spherical collapse and halo abundance calculations. This provides a unified framework connecting a reconstructed dark-energy sector and decaying dark matter (DDM) to the nonlinear formation of cosmic structures. We find that the reconstructed dark-energy equation of state can deviate from the $Λ$CDM value, $w=-1$, while the critical density threshold for collapse remains close to its standard prediction. The most pronounced signatures emerge in the abundance of massive halos, reflecting modifications to the growth of structure driven by both dark-matter decay and dynamical dark energy. By combining DESI DR1 clustering constraints with halo mass function measurements from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys DR9, we obtain joint constraints on the DDM lifetime and dark-energy parameters, demonstrating that halo abundances provide a powerful complementary probe of non-standard dark-sector physics.

AI.tldr: This paper combines decaying dark matter (DDM) with a reconstructed dark energy sector, using DESI DR1 data to constrain background evolution and propagating posteriors into nonlinear structure formation via spherical collapse and halo abundance calculations. Joint constraints with DESI Legacy Survey halo mass functions show halo abundances are a powerful probe of dark-sector physics.
AI.motivation: To investigate nonlinear structure formation in a cosmological model that simultaneously allows for decaying dark matter and a dynamically reconstructed dark energy sector, moving beyond the assumption of a cosmological constant.
AI.method: The authors construct a model where nonrelativistic dark matter decays into relativistic radiation (decay rate Γ=τ_ddm^{-1}) and reconstruct the dark energy sector directly from the expansion history using DESI DR1 BAO and compressed ShapeFit measurements. They propagate the posterior constraints into the nonlinear regime using spherical collapse and halo abundance calculations, then jointly constrain DDM lifetime and dark energy parameters using DESI DR1 clustering data and DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys DR9 halo mass function measurements.
AI.result: The reconstructed dark energy equation of state can deviate from w=-1 (ΛCDM), while the critical density threshold for collapse remains near the standard prediction. The strongest signatures appear in massive halo abundances, reflecting growth-of-structure modifications from both dark matter decay and dynamical dark energy.
AI.conclusion: Halo abundances provide a powerful complementary probe of non-standard dark-sector physics beyond what can be learned from background measurements alone, as demonstrated by joint constraints on DDM lifetime and dark energy parameters.

title: Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: a test case for environmental quenching
comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: To probe the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at intermediate redshift, we observed the CO(2-1) emission in the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at $z \sim 0.7$ with IRAM's NOEMA and 30m telescopes. This dense environment, located at the intersection of large-scale cosmic web filaments, has the specificity to host a large ($\sim 10^{4}$ kpc$^{2}$) ionized gas structure revealed by MUSE. We detect CO emission in four galaxies of the group at $\mathrm{S/N} > 5$ and derive upper limits for the remaining group members with secure spectroscopic redshifts. Stacked measurements indicate that group galaxies exhibit on average molecular gas contents reduced by $\sim 0.5$ dex relative to field scaling relations, corresponding to gas fractions that are $20\%$ to $40\%$ of those found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group. The 30m observations place an upper limit on the molecular gas associated with the extended ionized structure, $M_{\rm gas} < 2 \times 10^{10} \rm M_\odot$, implying that less than a third of the gas in the intra-group medium is in a cold, star-forming phase. Together, these results contribute to show how environmental mechanisms in dense group environments act to remove or suppress molecular gas within galaxies, capturing quenching processes in action.

AI.tldr: This study uses CO(2-1) observations of the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at z~0.7 to show that group galaxies have ~0.5 dex reduced molecular gas content compared to field galaxies, with gas fractions only 20-40% of typical main-sequence galaxies, while the extended ionized gas structure contains less than 2×10¹⁰ M☉ in cold molecular form.
AI.motivation: To probe the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at intermediate redshift, particularly in a dense environment located at the intersection of cosmic web filaments hosting a large ionized gas structure.
AI.method: Observed CO(2-1) emission in COSMOS-Gr30 at z~0.7 using IRAM's NOEMA and 30m telescopes; detected CO in four galaxies (S/N>5), derived upper limits for other members, and performed stacked measurements compared to field scaling relations.
AI.result: Group galaxies show ~0.5 dex reduced molecular gas content relative to field scaling relations, with gas fractions 20-40% of typical main-sequence galaxies; the extended ionized structure has M_gas < 2×10¹⁰ M☉, indicating less than a third of intra-group gas is in cold, star-forming phase.
AI.conclusion: Environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in group galaxies, and mechanisms in dense group environments act to remove or suppress molecular gas, capturing quenching processes in action.

title: Clustering of high-redshift quasars with DESI DR2
comment: 44 pages, 15 figures
summary: We present clustering measurements for high-redshift quasars using data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Data Release 2. Our sample consists of quasars with $2.0 < z < 3.5$ in the luminosity range $M_{1450} \leq -19.94$\,mag. We measure the mean quasar bias $b_Q(\bar{z} = 2.48) = 3.61 \pm 0.01$ for the full sample of $\sim 715,000$ quasars and quantify the redshift evolution of quasar bias by dividing the sample into four equal redshift bins. There is strong evolution of the quasar bias with redshift that is well fit by the function $b_Q(z) = a [(1 + z)^2 - 6.565] + b$ with $a=0.230 \pm 0.007$ and $b=2.394 \pm 0.035$, and this fit is also a good match to lower redshift measurements in the literature. This bias evolution is consistent with a characteristic halo mass of $\bar{M}_{\mathrm{h}} \sim 10^{12}\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$ that does not vary significantly with redshift. The inferred duty cycles for quasars in our sample are $f_{\mathrm{duty}} \sim 10^{-2}$, staying mostly constant over redshifts. We investigate the luminosity dependence of quasar clustering by dividing each of our four redshift bins into three luminosity bins. The size of our quasar sample permits the first statistically significant measurement of the luminosity dependence of quasar bias at these redshifts. We measure weak dependence of quasar bias on luminosity at fixed redshift, inconsistent with no dependence, but weaker than predicted by a model in which quasar luminosity is tightly correlated with halo mass. These clustering measurements provide a stringent test for models of active black hole light curves and the black hole-halo connection at high redshift.

AI.tldr: Using ~715,000 quasars from DESI DR2 at 2.0<z<3.5, we measure quasar bias b_Q=3.61±0.01 at z=2.48, find strong redshift evolution consistent with a constant characteristic halo mass ~10^12 M_sun and duty cycles ~10^{-2}, and detect weak but significant luminosity dependence of quasar clustering at high redshift for the first time.
AI.motivation: To understand the connection between quasars and their host dark matter halos, and to test models of black hole growth and active galactic nucleus light curves at high redshift using clustering measurements.
AI.method: Clustering measurements of ~715,000 quasars from DESI DR2 in the redshift range 2.0<z<3.5 and luminosity range M_1450 ≤ -19.94 mag. The sample is divided into four equal redshift bins and further subdivided into three luminosity bins per redshift bin to study luminosity dependence. Quasar bias is measured and modeled with a parametric function b_Q(z) = a[(1+z)^2 - 6.565] + b, and interpreted via the halo model to infer characteristic halo mass and duty cycles.
AI.result: Mean quasar bias b_Q(z=2.48)=3.61±0.01. Strong redshift evolution fitted with a=0.230±0.007, b=2.394±0.035. Characteristic halo mass ~10^12 M_sun with no significant redshift variation. Duty cycles ~10^{-2}, roughly constant over redshift. First statistically significant detection of luminosity dependence of quasar bias at these redshifts, though weaker than predicted by a model where luminosity tightly correlates with halo mass.
AI.conclusion: The clustering measurements provide stringent tests for models of active black hole light curves and the black hole-halo connection at high redshift; the weak luminosity dependence suggests that quasar luminosity is not solely determined by halo mass.

title: Probing the Nature of Lyman Continuum Emitting and Low-metallicity Galaxies Using the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Bait01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary:
The sources responsible for cosmic reionization remain a key open question in observational cosmology. Recent JWST results increasingly suggest that low-mass star-forming galaxies (e.g., compact starbursts and strong emission-line systems) dominated the ionizing photon budget. The physical mechanisms driving Lyman continuum (LyC) photon escape, including supernova, radiative, and cosmic-ray feedback, and the origin of extreme ionization conditions, remain poorly understood. Radio continuum (RC) emission, a well-established star-formation tracer in normal galaxies, is not yet well characterized in such extreme systems, which exhibit high star-formation rate densities, young stellar populations, low metallicity, and hard ionizing spectra.
  Targeted mid-frequency ($1-15$,GHz) observations with SKA precursors have begun probing low-redshift LyC emitters (LCEs), revealing links between RC spectral index, LyC escape fraction, ionization conditions, metallicity, and SFR surface density, alongwith deviations from the canonical RC$-$SFR relation. The higher sensitivity of the SKA Array Assemblies across Bands $\sim 1-5$ will enable systematic studies of fainter LCEs and low-mass, metal-poor galaxies. We present number density predictions for LCE candidates at $z \sim 1$-$3$, showing that SKA-Mid surveys can assemble samples of $\sim10-100$ candidates per square degree over a star-formation rate range of $1-100$,$M_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$, making a dedicated SKA Large Programme scientifically feasible.
  With the full SKA, in synergy with JWST and next generation telescopes, multi-wavelength analyses will robustly constrain the thermal and non-thermal RC components and cosmic-ray energy spectra, providing critical insights into the feedback processes governing LyC escape and star formation in the early universe.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the role of low-mass star-forming galaxies in cosmic reionization, focusing on how SKA observations of radio continuum emission can constrain Lyman continuum photon escape mechanisms. Current SKA precursor data show links between radio spectral index, LyC escape fraction, and galaxy properties. SKA-Mid surveys could detect ~10-100 LCE candidates per square degree at z~1-3. Full SKA combined with JWST and next-gen telescopes will enable multi-wavelength constraints on feedback processes governing LyC escape and early star formation.
AI.motivation: The sources responsible for cosmic reionization remain a key open question in observational cosmology. The physical mechanisms driving Lyman continuum photon escape and the origin of extreme ionization conditions are poorly understood, while radio continuum emission is not yet well characterized in the extreme low-mass, low-metallicity, high-SFR surface density systems thought to dominate reionization.
AI.method: Targeted mid-frequency (1-15 GHz) observations with SKA precursors probing low-redshift LyC emitters, along with number density predictions for LCE candidates at z~1-3 to assess SKA-Mid survey feasibility.
AI.result: Revealed links between RC spectral index, LyC escape fraction, ionization conditions, metallicity, and SFR surface density, along with deviations from the canonical RC-SFR relation. SKA-Mid surveys can assemble samples of ~10-100 candidates per square degree over an SFR range of 1-100 M⊙/yr.
AI.conclusion: A dedicated SKA Large Programme is scientifically feasible. With full SKA in synergy with JWST and next-gen telescopes, multi-wavelength analyses will robustly constrain thermal/non-thermal RC components and cosmic-ray energy spectra, providing critical insights into feedback processes governing LyC escape and star formation in the early universe.

title: Redshift-Dependent Intrinsic Dispersion in the Quasar UV/X-ray Luminosity Relation
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: Accurate modeling of the intrinsic dispersion in the quasar UV/X-ray luminosity relation is essential for reliable cosmological inference. We investigate its redshift dependence using luminosity distances reconstructed from cosmic chronometer and baryon acoustic oscillation measurements through Gaussian-process (GP) regression. Bayesian model comparison and posterior constraints show that the intrinsic dispersion is not well described by a single redshift-independent constant over $0.7<z<2.6$. It remains approximately constant at $0.7<z<1.6$, but shows an overall decreasing trend in the higher-redshift interval $1.6<z<2.6$, where the redshift-dependent intrinsic-dispersion model is decisively favored. This conclusion remains qualitatively robust against changes in the scaling-relation parameterization, GP kernel, and redshift binning scheme. We further examine its impact on cosmological inference in the flat $Λ$CDM model and find that, under the adopted calibration setup, the redshift-dependent intrinsic-dispersion model shifts the posterior median of $Ω_{\rm m0}$ by $ΔΩ_{\rm m0}\simeq 0.025$. This indicates that intrinsic-dispersion modeling is a non-negligible component of the systematic-error budget for quasar cosmology and should be accounted for in future precision analyses.

AI.tldr: The study investigates the redshift dependence of intrinsic dispersion in the quasar UV/X-ray luminosity relation using GP-reconstructed distances from cosmic chronometers and BAO. The dispersion is not constant over 0.7<z<2.6; it is approximately constant at lower redshifts but decreases at higher redshifts (1.6<z<2.6). This redshift-dependent modeling shifts the Ω_m0 posterior median by ~0.025, indicating it is a non-negligible systematic for quasar cosmology.
AI.motivation: Accurate modeling of intrinsic dispersion in the quasar UV/X-ray luminosity relation is essential for reliable cosmological inference, and its potential redshift dependence needs investigation.
AI.method: Gaussian-process regression is used to reconstruct luminosity distances from cosmic chronometer and BAO measurements. Bayesian model comparison and posterior constraints are applied to test redshift-independent vs. redshift-dependent intrinsic dispersion models across different redshift bins, scaling-relation parameterizations, and GP kernels.
AI.result: The intrinsic dispersion is not a single redshift-independent constant over 0.7<z<2.6; it remains approximately constant at 0.7<z<1.6 but decreases at 1.6<z<2.6, where the redshift-dependent model is decisively favored. The redshift-dependent model shifts Ω_m0 by ΔΩ_m0 ≈ 0.025.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic-dispersion modeling is a non-negligible systematic error component for quasar cosmology and should be accounted for in future precision analyses.

title: Columba: isolated dwarf galaxy populations in diverse cosmological environments simulated with a cold interstellar medium
comment: accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We introduce a suite of LambdaCDM cosmological, hydrodynamical simulations that track the evolution of a large population of dwarf galaxies. The suite comprises zoom-in simulations of 25 spherical, under-dense regions of r=5cMpc, selected to span $\approx1.5$ dex in mean enclosed density, covering voids to filamentary structures, whilst excluding haloes of Milky Way-mass or larger. The simulations achieve a mass resolution of $\sim 10^5$ solar masses with a galaxy formation model including cold, dense interstellar gas and whose subgrid stellar feedback efficiency reproduces the z=0 galaxy stellar mass function. We investigate the impact of the cosmic environment on dwarf galaxy formation and evolution. We find that the 5 cMpc environment influences the normalisation of the halo and galaxy mass functions, but does not significantly affect the stellar mass - halo mass (SMHM) relation and halo occupation fraction for galaxies with $M_{\star}=10^6-10^9$ solar masses. Instead, host halo concentration, estimated from DM-only counterparts, is more important: both the fraction of haloes hosting a resolved galaxy and the scatter about the SMHM relation correlate positively with concentration. Owing to halo assembly bias, concentration also influences galaxy formation times, such that at fixed halo mass more concentrated haloes host galaxies that are both older and more massive. The offset from the mean SMHM relation also anti-correlates with $t_{90}$, the time at which 90 percent of a galaxy's stellar mass has assembled. These correlations between halo properties and galaxy star formation histories present testable predictions for forthcoming observational surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper presents zoom-in cosmological hydrodynamical simulations of 25 under-dense regions (voids to filaments) at ~10^5 solar mass resolution, showing that the 5 cMpc environment affects mass function normalization but not the stellar mass-halo mass relation or halo occupation fraction, whereas halo concentration (via assembly bias) significantly influences these relations and galaxy formation times.
AI.motivation: To investigate the impact of the cosmic environment on dwarf galaxy formation and evolution using high-resolution simulations that capture a range of under-dense environments (voids to filaments) while excluding Milky Way-mass haloes.
AI.method: Suite of LambdaCDM cosmological hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations of 25 spherical under-dense regions (r=5 cMpc), spanning ~1.5 dex in mean enclosed density, with mass resolution ~10^5 solar masses and subgrid stellar feedback tuned to reproduce the z=0 stellar mass function.
AI.result: The 5 cMpc environment affects normalization of halo and galaxy mass functions but not the SMHM relation or halo occupation fraction for M_star=10^6-10^9 solar masses. Host halo concentration (from DM-only counterparts) correlates positively with halo occupation fraction and scatter in SMHM relation. Due to assembly bias, more concentrated haloes host older, more massive galaxies at fixed halo mass. Offset from mean SMHM anti-correlates with t_90.
AI.conclusion: Halo concentration, mediated by assembly bias, is a key driver of dwarf galaxy properties beyond the large-scale environment; correlations between halo properties and star formation histories provide testable predictions for future observational surveys.

title: Forward-modelling the Tolman and distance-duality tests with IllustrisTNG
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures; to be submitted to MNRAS
summary: The Tolman surface-brightness test and the angular-size distance-duality test are two complementary probes of the same underlying relation between luminosity and angular-diameter distance, $D_L = (1+z)^2 D_A$, as holds in any metric theory of gravity where photon number is conserved. Both tests have recently delivered a priori surprising signals: JWST/ASTRODEEP measurements yield a surface brightness scaling with redshift much flatter than the expected value, and ultracompact radio sources also appear to follow a flatter $D_L/D_A$ scaling with redshift. These results have been suggested to support non-expanding cosmologies, however they are also sensitive to astrophysical and instrumental effects. We test whether these results indicate genuine departures from standard cosmology by forward-modelling observed surface-brightness evolution in the IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulation, with an empirical mock-spectroscopic selection trained on ASTRODEEP. We show that the astrophysical evolution relevant for both tests may be effectively parametrised as a single power-law exponent for the luminosity density as a function of redshift, for which the simulation gives $γ=2.23\pm0.20$ across realistic aperture conventions. This value is approximately sufficient to explain both the Tolman and distance-duality signals within standard cosmology and galaxy formation physics, with a small discrepancy for the latter suggesting that radio AGN evolve slightly more strongly than bright galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using IllustrisTNG simulations, the paper shows that astrophysical evolution (parametrized as a power-law luminosity density with γ=2.23±0.20) can explain the apparently anomalous Tolman surface-brightness and angular-size distance-duality test signals within standard cosmology, without invoking non-expanding universes.
AI.motivation: Recent JWST/ASTRODEEP and ultracompact radio source observations have shown surface-brightness and distance-duality scalings flatter than expected from standard cosmology, leading some to suggest non-expanding cosmologies. The authors aim to test whether these signals genuinely depart from ΛCDM or can be explained by astrophysical and instrumental effects.
AI.method: Forward-modelling observed surface-brightness evolution in the IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulation, with an empirical mock-spectroscopic selection trained on ASTRODEEP data. The astrophysical evolution is parametrized as a single power-law exponent γ for luminosity density as a function of redshift.
AI.result: The simulation yields γ=2.23±0.20 across realistic aperture conventions. This value approximately explains both the Tolman and distance-duality signals within standard cosmology. A small discrepancy for the distance-duality test suggests radio AGN evolve slightly more strongly than bright galaxies.
AI.conclusion: The apparent deviations from standard cosmology in both tests can be largely attributed to astrophysical evolution of galaxy properties rather than requiring non-expanding cosmologies, though radio AGN evolution may be slightly stronger.

title: UV Star-Formation Rates of the SHIELD Dwarf Galaxies
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures. Paper accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The Survey of HI in Extremely Low-mass Dwarfs (SHIELD) is a multi-wavelength observational project targeting gas-rich, star-forming dwarf galaxies at the faint end of the HI mass function. We present near-ultraviolet (NUV) and far-ultraviolet (FUV) flux measurements obtained from GALEX survey images and use these fluxes to derive FUV star-formation rates (SFRs) for all 75 SHIELD galaxies with GALEX data. This paper represents the first published analysis that makes use of the full SHIELD sample. We compare the FUV SFRs to a variety of physical quantities to better understand the nature of SHIELD galaxies. When comparing the H$α$ SFRs to the FUV SFRs for SHIELD and other local galaxy surveys, we confirm and solidify previous results that show that H$α$-based SFRs for dwarf galaxies can grossly underestimate the true rate of star formation, emphasizing the highly stochastic nature of star formation in extremely low-mass galaxies. We further show that FUV SFRs appear to be robust tracers of star formation down to the very lowest galaxy masses included in this study. We show that baryonic mass is the best mass-related tracer for the prediction of the FUV SFR of the galaxies in our sample. Not surprisingly, the SHIELD dwarf galaxies exhibit long gas-depletion timescales and large gas mass fractions: fully 68% of the SHIELD galaxies have gas masses that are larger than their stellar masses.

AI.tldr: The SHIELD project analyzes UV fluxes from GALEX for 75 low-mass dwarf galaxies, finding that Hα-based SFRs underestimate true star formation in dwarfs, while FUV SFRs are robust tracers. Baryonic mass best predicts FUV SFR, and 68% of SHIELD galaxies have gas masses exceeding stellar masses, indicating long gas-depletion timescales.
AI.motivation: To understand the star formation properties of extremely low-mass dwarf galaxies at the faint end of the HI mass function using multi-wavelength observations from the SHIELD project, particularly investigating the reliability of different SFR tracers in low-mass regimes.
AI.method: NUV and FUV flux measurements from GALEX survey images were used to derive FUV-based SFRs for 75 SHIELD galaxies. These were compared to Hα-based SFRs and other physical quantities across the full SHIELD sample.
AI.result: Hα-based SFRs significantly underestimate true star formation in dwarf galaxies due to stochasticity; FUV SFRs are robust tracers down to the lowest masses; baryonic mass is the best predictor of FUV SFR; 68% of SHIELD galaxies have gas masses > stellar masses, with long gas-depletion timescales.
AI.conclusion: FUV-based SFRs are more reliable than Hα-based SFRs for extremely low-mass dwarf galaxies, and these galaxies are gas-dominated with long depletion times, highlighting the stochastic nature of star formation at low masses.

title: Methodological Frontiers in 21-cm Intensity Mapping: the Treatment of Systematics and Foreground Contamination
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Spinelli01
summary:
The distribution of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the post-reionization universe traces the cosmic large-scale structure and therefore serves as a powerful cosmological probe. An efficient way to measure its distribution over wide sky areas and redshift ranges is through single-dish intensity mapping, which exploits the autocorrelation signal of each dish in a telescope array while scanning the same sky patch. Thanks to its broad frequency coverage and technical capabilities, SKA-Mid will enable measurements of the integrated 21 cm emission from HI up to redshift $z\sim3$, making single-dish intensity mapping a key observable for probing dark matter and dark energy.
  Isolating the faint 21 cm cosmological signal without introducing biases is, however, challenging. The 21 cm signal is several orders of magnitude weaker than the astrophysical foregrounds, and its analysis is further affected by instrumental systematics. Overcoming these difficulties requires detailed modelling together with continuous improvements and innovations in data-analysis techniques. Over the past decade, the international community has developed and tested new methods to address current observational challenges and prepare for forthcoming SKA-Mid observations.
  This chapter reviews recent advances in map-making and component-separation techniques, with particular emphasis on telescope-specific systematics such as beam response and correlated noise. We focus on results obtained in controlled simulation environments, providing a valuable framework for assessing the strengths and limitations of different approaches.
  Developing robust algorithms capable of accurately handling instrumental effects and sky-model uncertainties is a crucial step toward fully exploiting the cosmological potential of HI intensity-mapping surveys in the SKA Observatory era.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews recent advances in map-making and component-separation techniques for single-dish HI intensity mapping with SKA-Mid, focusing on telescope-specific systematics (beam response, correlated noise) and results from controlled simulations, aiming to isolate the faint 21 cm signal from overwhelming foregrounds and instrumental effects.
AI.motivation: Single-dish HI intensity mapping with SKA-Mid can probe dark matter and dark energy up to z~3, but the 21 cm signal is orders of magnitude weaker than foregrounds and affected by instrumental systematics, requiring advanced data-analysis techniques to avoid biases.
AI.method: The chapter reviews map-making and component-separation techniques developed over the past decade, with emphasis on handling telescope-specific systematics (beam response, correlated noise) in controlled simulation environments to assess strengths and limitations of different approaches.
AI.result: The review presents results from controlled simulation environments that test various algorithms for accurately handling instrumental effects and sky-model uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Developing robust algorithms for instrumental effects and sky-model uncertainties is crucial for fully exploiting the cosmological potential of HI intensity-mapping surveys in the SKA Observatory era.

title: Predicted Capabilities of the SPRITE SmallSat for a Low-Redshift Lyman Continuum Emission Survey
comment: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Astronomical Telescopes, Instruments, and Systems on June 22, 2026. 30 pages with 17 figures and 3 tables
summary: Ionizing Lyman continuum (LyC; $λ< 912~\rm{\mathring{A}}$) radiation from low-redshift ($z \sim 0.3$) galaxies provides crucial insight into the processes that contributed to cosmic reionization. While the \textit{James Webb Space Telescope} has observed galaxies at redshifts as high as $z \sim 14$, detecting LyC beyond $z \sim 3$ is challenging due to absorption by neutral hydrogen in the intergalactic medium (IGM). Low-redshift LyC emitters (LCEs), therefore, act as proxies for their high-redshift counterparts, enabling direct measurements of LyC escape fractions with reduced IGM interference.
