These observations allow detailed ancillary studies of galaxy properties and the mechanisms driving ionizing photon escape, which cannot be directly observed at the Epoch of Reionization. This paper examines the capabilities of the Supernova remnants and Proxies for Re-Ionization Testbed Experiment (SPRITE) SmallSat, designed to study LyC emission from star-forming galaxies at $0.16 < z < 0.4$. SPRITE uses advanced mirror coatings and a highly sensitive far-ultraviolet imaging spectrograph, enabling it to probe LyC from galaxies that have been difficult to study with prior and existing instruments. To assess SPRITE's predicted performance in LyC studies, we select eight previously confirmed LCEs from the Low-redshift Lyman Continuum Survey as commissioning targets. Observations of these commissioning LCEs will validate SPRITE's LyC sensitivity and characterize its detection limits. This will enable the broader SPRITE low-redshift LCE survey, which will provide new constraints on the physics of LyC escape and help bridge the gap between low- and high-redshift LyC studies. SPRITE will also inform the design and scientific potential of future Lyman-UV missions, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the SPRITE SmallSat mission's capability to study Lyman continuum escape from star-forming galaxies at z~0.3 as proxies for cosmic reionization sources. It validates SPRITE's performance using eight known LCEs from the Low-redshift Lyman Continuum Survey as commissioning targets, aiming to bridge low- and high-redshift LyC studies and inform future missions like the Habitable Worlds Observatory.
AI.motivation: Low-redshift LyC emitters serve as accessible proxies for high-redshift galaxies that reionized the universe, as direct LyC detection at the Epoch of Reionization (z>3) is obscured by IGM neutral hydrogen absorption. The paper aims to validate SPRITE's unique capability to observe LyC from galaxies that previous instruments could not study effectively.
AI.method: The study selects eight previously confirmed LCEs from the Low-redshift Lyman Continuum Survey as commissioning targets. SPRITE uses advanced mirror coatings and a highly sensitive far-ultraviolet imaging spectrograph to observe LyC at 0.16<z<0.4. Observations of commissioning targets will validate sensitivity and characterize detection limits.
AI.result: SPRITE is predicted to successfully probe LyC from galaxies that have been challenging for prior instruments. Commissioning observations will confirm its LyC sensitivity and establish detection limits, enabling a broader low-redshift LCE survey.
AI.conclusion: SPRITE will provide new constraints on LyC escape physics, bridging low- and high-redshift LyC studies. It will inform the design of future Lyman-UV missions, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

title: A solid unification of the dark sector
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures
summary: We construct a unified description of dark matter and dark energy in terms of a single dark component that behaves as a pressureless fluid in the early Universe and undergoes a transition to a solid phase at late times that can support accelerated expansion. A generalized Chaplygin-type solid provides a simple realization of this scenario. The solid nature of the dark medium prevents the instabilities and strong acoustic oscillations that typically arise in perfect-fluid unifications. It also gives rise to distinctive signatures in cosmological perturbations, such as a suppression of structure growth, a nontrivial gravitational slip, and an effective mass for gravitational waves. Since these effects share a common origin in the solid phase, they become relevant only at low redshifts, leaving the high-redshift cosmology essentially unmodified. This demonstrates that a solidly unified dark sector can reproduce the desired background transition from dark matter to dark energy while yielding testable imprints in cosmological perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified dark sector model where a single component transitions from a pressureless fluid (dark matter-like) at early times to a solid phase at late times (dark energy-like), using a generalized Chaplygin-type solid to avoid instabilities and produce testable signatures in cosmological perturbations.
AI.motivation: To construct a unified description of dark matter and dark energy as a single dark component, overcoming the instabilities and strong acoustic oscillations that plague perfect-fluid unification models.
AI.method: The authors use a generalized Chaplygin-type solid to realize a dark component that transitions from a pressureless fluid phase (early Universe) to a solid phase (late times) capable of supporting accelerated expansion.
AI.result: The solid nature prevents instabilities and strong acoustic oscillations; produces distinctive signatures including suppression of structure growth, nontrivial gravitational slip, and an effective mass for gravitational waves — all relevant only at low redshifts.
AI.conclusion: A solidly unified dark sector can reproduce the background transition from dark matter to dark energy while yielding testable imprints in cosmological perturbations, leaving high-redshift cosmology unmodified.

title: Cm-wavelength Studies of Molecular Gas and Star Formation at High Redshift with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/RanWang01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The Square Kilometre Array will be a revolutionary instrument for the study of gas in the distant Universe. At frequencies below ~50 GHz, observations of redshifted emission from low-J transitions of CO, HCN, HCO+, and HNC, etc. provide insight into the kinematics and mass budget of the cold, dense star-forming gas in galaxies. Over the past decade, sensitive imaging using ALMA has detected and resolved the redshifted high-J molecular CO line emission and far-infrared fine structure lines in samples of galaxies over a wide redshift range, shedding light on active star-formation processes at the early epoch of galaxy evolution. In recent years, increasing numbers of young galaxies at high redshift are discovered by JWST, which significantly improved our knowledge of different galaxy populations across cosmic time. In this updated chapter of the SKA science book, we would like to highlight the importance of studies of the low-J molecular lines in high-z galaxies using SKA toward high frequencies, discussing the request of frequency coverage beyond 15 GHz and emphasizing its crucial role in exploring the cold molecular gas content in the young galaxy populations in the early universe and investigating the regions of active-star formation using molecular CO and various dense gas tracers.

AI.tldr: This SKA science book chapter highlights the importance of observing low-J molecular lines (CO, HCN, HCO+, HNC) at frequencies above 15 GHz with SKA to study cold molecular gas and star formation in high-redshift galaxies, complementing ALMA's high-J CO and JWST's discovery of young galaxies.
AI.motivation: To underscore the critical need for SKA frequency coverage beyond 15 GHz to probe cold molecular gas in high-z galaxies, complementing existing ALMA (high-J CO, far-infrared lines) and JWST (young galaxy populations) observations, thereby enabling a complete picture of gas and star formation across cosmic time.
AI.method: Review of low-J molecular line observations (CO, HCN, HCO+, HNC) as cold dense gas tracers; discussion of SKA's high-frequency capabilities (>15 GHz) for redshifted emission; integration with ALMA high-J CO/far-infrared data and JWST galaxy discovery.
AI.result: The chapter demonstrates that SKA's high-frequency coverage is essential to probe cold molecular gas reservoirs in early-universe galaxies, trace active star-formation regions via CO and dense gas tracers, and fill the observational gap left by ALMA (high-J lines) and JWST (optical/NIR galaxy identification).
AI.conclusion: SKA's extended frequency coverage above 15 GHz is crucial for advancing our understanding of cold molecular gas content and star formation in young high-redshift galaxies, and should be prioritized in the SKA science program.

title: HALO II: Constraining Hubble constant $H_{0}$ through continuum delay fitting of Fairall 9
comment: Submitted to A&A, 19 pages, 11 figures, and 2 tables
summary: The Hubble tension remains one of the most significant unresolved problems in modern cosmology. A key question is whether it may arise from underestimated systematic uncertainties in the different measurement techniques. In this context, new independent methods are of exceptional importance. We therefore pursue a novel approach to determining the Hubble constant, $H_{0}$ based on continuum time delay and spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Unlike conventional techniques, this method is entirely independent of the cosmic distance ladder and does not require cross-calibration against other distance indicators. As a result, it enables a direct determination of $H_{0}$, free from the arbitrary normalizations that often affect indirect measurements. We conducted a dedicated monitoring campaign of the Seyfert galaxy Fairall 9 and further developed the {\tt H0RIZON-AGN} model to interpret the resulting observations. The model incorporates the effects of radiation reprocessing in the surrounding cold accretion disk, enabling a more realistic description of the observed continuum delays. Through the simultaneous modeling of the continuum lag-spectrum and the broadband SED of Fairall 9, we derived a Hubble constant of $H_{0}=72.4_{-3.7}^{+3.4} \, \rm km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}$. Achieving a measurement precision of approximately 5% from a single source demonstrates the considerable potential of this method for independent determinations of the Hubble constant. Our determination of $H_{0}$ is broadly consistent, within the current uncertainties, with both early- and late-Universe measurements. Future applications of the method to larger datasets, particularly those provided by the Vera Rubin Observatory, are expected to reduce the uncertainty to below 1%, thereby establishing this approach as a powerful independent probe of the Hubble tension.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a novel method for measuring the Hubble constant using continuum time delay and SED modeling in AGNs, independent of the cosmic distance ladder. Applying this method to Fairall 9 yields H₀ = 72.4⁺³·⁴₋₃·₇ km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ (~5% precision), broadly consistent with both early- and late-Universe measurements. Future application to larger datasets (e.g., Vera Rubin Observatory) could reduce uncertainty below 1%.
AI.motivation: The Hubble tension remains a major unresolved problem in cosmology. New independent methods for measuring H₀ are critically needed to determine whether the discrepancy arises from systematic uncertainties in existing measurement techniques.
AI.method: The authors developed the H0RIZON-AGN model to simultaneously fit the continuum lag-spectrum and broadband SED of the Seyfert galaxy Fairall 9. The model incorporates radiation reprocessing in the cold accretion disk, enabling a direct determination of H₀ independent of the cosmic distance ladder and without cross-calibration against other distance indicators.
AI.result: The measurement yields H₀ = 72.4⁺³·⁴₋₃·₇ km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, achieving approximately 5% precision from a single AGN source.
AI.conclusion: The result is broadly consistent with both early- and late-Universe measurements within current uncertainties. The method shows considerable potential as an independent probe of the Hubble tension, and future application to larger datasets (e.g., from the Vera Rubin Observatory) could reduce uncertainties to below 1%.

title: Search for Seeds of The Cradle of Stars: Study of The Evolution From Atomic to Molecular Hydrogen Clouds with 1000 AU Scale Resolution
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Yamamoto01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The aim of this science case for SKA1-Mid is to elucidate the spatial and velocity structure of the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) on scales below the Field length, thereby elucidating the physical processes that govern CNM structure formation and its role in the earliest stages of molecular cloud formation. This goal will be achieved through a unique observational combination of several-arcsecond angular resolution, high velocity resolution, and unprecedented surface-brightness sensitivity. These observations will reveal the characteristic size, morphology, velocity structure, and internal dynamics of CNM clumps, and will directly connect such structures to the earliest phases of the atomic to molecular transition. Full-polarization observations with SKA1-Mid will also enable emission-based Zeeman measurements of the CNM, allowing the magnetic field strength to be mapped and opening a new window on the role of magnetic fields in CNM formation and evolution. In particular, this will make it possible to determine whether magnetic fields primarily inhibit fragmentation by supporting the gas against compression, or instead guide anisotropic condensation and promote the development of small-scale CNM structure through thermal instability. In combination with interferometric spatial filtering and high spectral resolution, SKA1-Mid will selectively trace the CNM and robustly identify individual clumps in both position and velocity space. These capabilities will provide decisive tests of thermal instability and the two-phase turbulence model, and will establish a new observational foundation for understanding how molecular clouds emerge from the multi-phase atomic interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using SKA1-Mid to observe the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) at sub-Field-length scales with high angular/velocity resolution and sensitivity, to study its structure, magnetic fields via Zeeman measurements, and its role in the atomic-to-molecular transition and molecular cloud formation.
AI.motivation: To elucidate the spatial and velocity structure of the CNM on scales below the Field length, understand the physical processes governing CNM structure formation, and clarify its role in the earliest stages of molecular cloud formation.
AI.method: SKA1-Mid observations combining several-arcsecond angular resolution, high velocity resolution, and unprecedented surface-brightness sensitivity; full-polarization Zeeman measurements to map magnetic field strengths; interferometric spatial filtering and high spectral resolution to selectively trace CNM and identify individual clumps in position-velocity space.
AI.result: Revealing characteristic size, morphology, velocity structure, and internal dynamics of CNM clumps; direct connection of structures to the earliest atomic-to-molecular transition; mapping of magnetic field strength via emission-based Zeeman measurements.
AI.conclusion: SKA1-Mid will provide decisive tests of thermal instability and the two-phase turbulence model, establish a new observational foundation for understanding molecular cloud emergence from the multi-phase atomic ISM, and determine whether magnetic fields inhibit fragmentation or guide anisotropic condensation promoting small-scale CNM structure.

title: Extended Structure in E+A Galaxies Via Image Stacking
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures
summary: Small-scale interactions such as minor mergers, flybys and harassment are considered common driving mechanisms that can both initiate and quench star-forming processes within post-starburst (PSB) galaxies. PSBs have been linked to disturbed morphologies and faint tidal features in numerous works. We aim to independently study these features in E+A galaxies found in the Galaxy and Mass Assembly Fourth Data Release (GAMA DR4). Using image stacking techniques, we derive the averaged radial surface brightness profiles of E+A image stacks alongside the Sérsic parameters that best fit these profiles. These E+A stacks consist of 57 images extracted from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) in g, r & i bands. The E+A stacks are shown to have brighter extended regions than similar non-PSB galaxies, which is indicative of faint tidal features that could be caused by small-scale interactions. Additionally, we make use of Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Legacy Survey imaging, which is deeper than SDSS, to further support our conclusions and find that the Legacy Survey images independently strengthen the evidence for excess light at extended radii relative to the comparison samples. We discuss these findings in the context of future surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) survey.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes E+A (post-starburst) galaxies from GAMA DR4 using image stacking of 57 SDSS images, finding they have brighter extended regions than non-PSB galaxies, indicating faint tidal features from small-scale interactions. Deeper DESI Legacy Survey images independently confirm excess light at extended radii. Results are discussed in context of future LSST surveys.
AI.motivation: Small-scale interactions (minor mergers, flybys, harassment) are thought to drive star formation quenching in post-starburst galaxies, which have been linked to disturbed morphologies and tidal features. The authors aim to independently study these features in E+A galaxies.
AI.method: Image stacking of 57 E+A galaxy images from SDSS (g, r, i bands) from GAMA DR4, deriving averaged radial surface brightness profiles and fitting Sérsic parameters. Additional validation using deeper DESI Legacy Survey imaging.
AI.result: E+A stacks show brighter extended regions than comparable non-PSB galaxies, indicating faint tidal features likely caused by small-scale interactions. DESI Legacy Survey data independently confirms excess light at extended radii.
AI.conclusion: The findings support that small-scale interactions drive the post-starburst phase in these galaxies. Future surveys like LSST will enable further investigation of these faint tidal features.

title: SKA VLBI survey of the Southern sky for astrometry, geodesy, and astrophysics
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/MingHuiXu01
summary: The development of SKA will open the opportunity to run dedicated VLBI surveys of the Southern sky and observe sources not visible at radio telescopes located in the Northern hemisphere. These surveys will allow for doing geodesy with a Southern hemisphere-centered network, increase the density of compact radio sources that can be used as calibrators, further extend the celestial reference frame to deep south, and facilitate high-precision differential astrometry for a wide range of applications. Achieving a deep completeness level and determining the parsec-scale properties of extragalactic radio sources is crucial for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger astrophysics. This includes supporting Cherenkov and neutrino telescope science cases, as well as joint VLBI-Gaia studies of active galaxies.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses how the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will enable dedicated VLBI surveys of the Southern sky, supporting geodesy, celestial reference frame extension, calibrator source density increase, and high-precision differential astrometry for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger astrophysics, including Cherenkov/neutrino telescopes and VLBI-Gaia studies.
AI.motivation: To leverage the SKA's Southern sky capabilities for dedicated VLBI surveys, addressing the current lack of deep, high-resolution observations of Southern extragalactic radio sources for geodesy, astrometry, and multi-messenger astrophysics.
AI.method: Proposed dedicated VLBI surveys using the SKA to observe Southern sky sources, combined with analysis of parsec-scale source properties, completeness levels, and integration with multi-wavelength (Cherenkov, neutrino) and astrometric (Gaia) datasets.
AI.result: Enables Southern hemisphere-centered geodetic networks, increases calibrator source density, extends the celestial reference frame to deep southern declinations, and facilitates high-precision differential astrometry.
AI.conclusion: SKA-driven VLBI surveys are essential for achieving deep completeness of Southern extragalactic sources, supporting multi-messenger astrophysics (Cherenkov, neutrino telescopes) and joint VLBI-Gaia studies of active galaxies.

title: NO molecule in massive star forming regions
summary: Context. Among diatomic molecules composed of the abundant elements C, N and O, NO has been detected far less than the well studied CN and CO, making it a crucial yet under-observed component in nitrogen-containing chemical networks. NO was thought to serve as a potential tracer of shocks, as evidenced with orders abundance enhancements reported in literature. Aims. Large-sample observations for NO molecule in widespread interstellar environments are needed to confirm if the enhancement of NO is due to shock chemistry or not. Methods. Single-point survey for NO lines around 150 GHz was carried out by Arizona Radio Observatory 12-meter telescope towards a sample of 36 massive star forming regions containing SiO emission, which include three evolutionary stages: 4 IRDCs, 6 protostars and 26 H II regions. Results. The NO emission was detected in 28 sources with a detection rate of 78%. Beam-averaged NO column densities and abundances relative to H2 were derived from integrated intensities of two main hyperfine lines. Correlations between NO and SiO in integrated intensity and relative abundance are similar to the corresponding correlations of c-C3H2, indicating that NO enrichment may not significantly involve pronounced shock activities, which coincides with the trend in line widths: NO is close to c-C3H2, both smaller than H2CO and far smaller than SiO. Conclusions. Observational evidence does not strongly support significant NO enhancement by shock chemistry in the observed sources, indicating that the formation of NO does not necessarily require shocks.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys NO (nitric oxide) emission towards 36 massive star-forming regions and finds a 78% detection rate. By comparing NO with shock tracer SiO and other molecules, the authors conclude that NO formation does not necessarily require shock chemistry, contrary to previous assumptions.
AI.motivation: NO has been under-observed compared to CN and CO in interstellar environments, yet it is a crucial component of nitrogen-containing chemical networks. Previous literature reported order-of-magnitude abundance enhancements of NO thought to be associated with shocks, but large-sample observations across diverse environments were lacking to confirm this connection.
AI.method: Single-point survey of NO lines around 150 GHz using the Arizona Radio Observatory 12-meter telescope toward a sample of 36 massive star-forming regions containing SiO emission, spanning three evolutionary stages: 4 infrared dark clouds (IRDCs), 6 protostars, and 26 H II regions.
AI.result: NO emission detected in 28 out of 36 sources (78% detection rate). Beam-averaged NO column densities and abundances relative to H₂ were derived from integrated intensities of two main hyperfine lines. Correlations between NO and SiO in integrated intensity and relative abundance are similar to those of c-C₃H₂, not showing pronounced shock signatures. NO line widths are close to c-C₃H₂, both smaller than H₂CO and far smaller than SiO.
AI.conclusion: Observational evidence does not strongly support significant NO enhancement by shock chemistry in the observed sources; NO formation does not necessarily require shocks.

title: Semi-empirical Predictions for Ultra-deep Radio Counts of Star-forming Galaxies with the SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Giulietti01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Star-forming galaxies (SFGs) dominate the faint radio sky at flux densities below 0.1 mJy. Identifying these systems through a multiwavelength approach is essential to tracing the cosmic history of star formation. Upcoming surveys with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) in its AA4 configuration for the Mid array will probe these faint populations, offering unprecedented insights into the star formation activity of galaxies across cosmic time. Semi-empirical models, built on minimal assumptions and empirical galaxy relations, provide an efficient framework to study galaxy evolution using recent radio and optical/near-infrared (NIR) data. We developed SEMPER (Semi-EMPirical model for Extragalactic Radio emission) to predict the radio luminosity functions and number counts of SFGs. SEMPER combines redshift-dependent stellar mass functions from deep NIR surveys with empirical relations such as the galaxy main sequence and the IR/radio correlation, to characterise the radio properties of massive, high-redshift galaxies. The model shows excellent agreement with recent deep radio observations and naturally predicts a substantial population of massive, dust-obscured galaxies already in place at early epochs. In this chapter, we extend the SEMPER framework to SKA surveys by including an evolving starburst fraction and computing differential number counts at 1.4 GHz for both lensed and unlensed SFGs. Furthermore, we predict the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) traced by radio-emitting galaxies up to $z\approx10$. Our results show that SKA surveys will probe the faintest flux-density regimes, dominated by galaxies powered by star formation, and that <20 hours of SKA-Mid Band 2 observations will recover at least $\approx$20% of the total SFRD predicted by SEMPER, including contributions from optically/NIR-dark systems up to $z\approx 6$.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SEMPER, a semi-empirical model predicting radio emission from star-forming galaxies, and forecasts that SKA-Mid surveys with <20 hours of Band 2 observations can recover ~20% of the cosmic star formation rate density up to z≈6, including optically/NIR-dark galaxies.
AI.motivation: To understand the cosmic history of star formation by identifying faint star-forming galaxies (<0.1 mJy) using upcoming SKA radio surveys, bridging the gap between deep radio observations and galaxy evolution models.
AI.method: Developed SEMPER (Semi-EMPirical model for Extragalactic Radio emission), combining redshift-dependent stellar mass functions from deep NIR surveys with empirical relations (galaxy main sequence, IR/radio correlation) to predict radio luminosity functions and number counts, including evolving starburst fraction and gravitational lensing effects.
AI.result: SEMPER agrees well with deep radio observations; predicts a substantial population of massive, dust-obscured galaxies at early epochs; shows SKA surveys will probe the faintest flux-density regimes; <20 hours of SKA-Mid Band 2 observations will recover ≥20% of the total SFRD up to z≈6, including optically/NIR-dark systems.
AI.conclusion: SKA-Mid surveys will be highly effective at tracing cosmic star formation history via radio emission from faint SFGs, recovering significant SFRD from dust-obscured populations inaccessible to optical/NIR surveys.

title: Validating the ICCF-Cut Method with Simultaneous Photometric and Spectroscopic H$α$ Reverberation Mapping of NGC 4151 and UGC 3374
comment: 24 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Photometric reverberation mapping (RM) provides an efficient alternative to spectroscopic RM for probing the broad-line region (BLR) sizes in AGNs. In our previous work, we proposed the ICCF-Cut method, which extracts H$α$ emission-line variability from broadband photometric light curves and measures the lags to estimate the BLR sizes. To further assess the reliability of this method, we conduct simultaneous photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of two nearby Seyfert galaxies, NGC 4151 and UGC 3374, over multiple observing seasons using the Lijiang 2.4 m telescope. By directly comparing the photometric and spectroscopic RM results in each season, we find that the extracted H$α$ light curves using the ICCF-Cut method closely resemble those derived from spectroscopy. The photometric H$α$ lags are also generally consistent with the spectroscopic H$α$ lags within the uncertainties. For several seasons where the photometric H$α$ lags are slightly underestimated, we find that the discrepancy may be caused by residual He\,\textsc{i} contamination in the extracted H$α$ light curves. After correcting for this contamination, the photometric lag measurements become more consistent with the spectroscopic results. We further explore the performance of the ICCF-Cut method using the simulated light curves with different filter bandwidths. For our observational and simulated cases, the method can successfully recover the emission-line variability and lag measurements broadly consistent with the spectroscopic results. This provides further support for the applicability of the ICCF-Cut method in photometric RM.

AI.tldr: The ICCF-Cut method extracts Hα emission-line variability from broadband photometric light curves for reverberation mapping. By comparing photometric and spectroscopic RM of NGC 4151 and UGC 3374, the method yields consistent results, with minor discrepancies due to He I contamination, correctable with additional correction.
AI.motivation: To assess the reliability of the ICCF-Cut method for photometric reverberation mapping by directly comparing photometric and spectroscopic RM results for nearby AGNs.
AI.method: Simultaneous photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of NGC 4151 and UGC 3374 using the Lijiang 2.4 m telescope; application of ICCF-Cut to extract Hα light curves from broadband photometry; comparison of extracted Hα variability and lags with spectroscopic measurements; simulation of light curves with different filter bandwidths to further test the method.
AI.result: Photometric Hα light curves resemble spectroscopic ones; photometric Hα lags are generally consistent with spectroscopic lags within uncertainties; slight underestimation in some seasons is attributable to residual He I contamination, correctable with additional correction; simulations confirm the method recovers emission-line variability and lags broadly consistent with spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: The ICCF-Cut method is a reliable approach for photometric reverberation mapping, providing results consistent with spectroscopic RM, and its applicability is supported by both observational and simulated tests.

title: Feeding and Feedback in Dwarf Galaxies (FeeD) -- I. Evidence of nuclear ultra-fast and galaxy-scale outflows in the dwarf galaxy Arp 151
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, Accepted for publication in A&A Letters
summary: Feeding and feedback regulated by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) play a central role in galaxy growth and evolution, yet these processes remain poorly understood in low-mass galaxies. In particular, the presence, properties, and role of ultra-fast nuclear outflows (UFOs) in low-mass galaxy systems are largely unexplored. We analyze available NuSTAR X-ray observations of Arp 151 and find a possible evidence ($\sim 2σ$ confidence) for a fast outflow with a velocity of $\sim0.18c$ from the central BH. Furthermore, we have also detected an optical galaxy-scale outflow in MaNGA Integral Field Unit data. The estimated nuclear and galaxy-scale mass outflow rates are $\sim0.015$ $M_\odot$/yr from {\it NuSTAR} and $\sim0.43$ $M_\odot$/yr from MaNGA, respectively. Our estimates suggest that such outflows may significantly regulate the feedback process in the galaxy. Comparing the kinetics of the UFO and the galaxy-scale outflow indicates that they are in the momentum-conserving phase. This tentative detection implies that dwarf galaxies are also able to generate UFOs, which so far have been detected in massive galaxies. Thus, the AGN feedback may also be important for the evolution of the dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents tentative evidence (~2σ) for an ultra-fast outflow (UFO) of ~0.18c from the SMBH in the low-mass galaxy Arp 151 using NuSTAR X-ray data, alongside an optical galaxy-scale outflow detected in MaNGA IFU data. The nuclear and galaxy-scale mass outflow rates are ~0.015 M⊙/yr and ~0.43 M⊙/yr, respectively, suggesting the outflows are in a momentum-conserving phase and may significantly regulate feedback, implying that AGN-driven UFOs and feedback could be important even in dwarf galaxies.
AI.motivation: To investigate the presence, properties, and role of ultra-fast nuclear outflows (UFOs) in low-mass galaxies, a regime where such AGN-driven outflows remain largely unexplored despite their known importance in massive galaxy evolution.
AI.method: Analysis of NuSTAR X-ray observations to search for UFO signatures (absorption features indicating velocities ~0.18c) in Arp 151, supplemented by MaNGA Integral Field Unit data to detect and characterize the optical galaxy-scale outflow; mass outflow rates are estimated from both datasets and compared kinematically.
AI.result: Possible detection (~2σ confidence) of a UFO with velocity ~0.18c, nuclear mass outflow rate ~0.015 M⊙/yr; detection of an optical galaxy-scale outflow with mass outflow rate ~0.43 M⊙/yr; kinetic comparison suggests the outflows are in a momentum-conserving phase.
AI.conclusion: Low-mass/dwarf galaxies like Arp 151 can host UFOs previously only seen in massive galaxies, implying that AGN feedback processes may also be significant for the evolution of dwarf galaxies.

title: Probing outflow physics through CH$_3$CN and CH$_3$OH chemistry
summary: Chemical correlations between molecules provide powerful diagnostics to probe the physical conditions of protostellar outflows. In particular, the relationship between methanol (CH$_3$OH) and methyl cyanide (CH$_3$CN) offers a promising tool to investigate the chemistry and irradiation environment of shocked gas. In this Letter, we use the CH$_3$OH/CH$_3$CN abundance ratio to constrain the physical properties of the outflow driven by the Class 0 protostar S68N using ALMA Band 3 and Band 6 observations. Assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), we derive excitation temperatures of 50-60 K and column densities of 2-3$\times$10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$ for CH$_3$CN and 3-5$\times$10$^{15}$ cm$^{-2}$ for CH$_3$OH. The resulting CH$_3$OH/CH$_3$CN abundance ratio is nearly constant along the outflow, with values of $\sim$100-200, similar to those found in other protostellar environments. Using an up-to-date astrochemical model, we test whether gas-phase formation of CH$_3$CN can account for the observed ratios. We find that they are reproduced only by assuming enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates $ζ_{\rm CR}$ up to $\sim$10$^{-14}$ s$^{-1}$. These results suggest that the CH$_3$OH-CH$_3$CN correlation can be used as a probe of the irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows. Further studies are required to explore the possible contribution of grain-surface formation of CH$_3$CN which could lead to a lower $ζ_{\rm CR}$ and to extend the analysis to a larger sample of sources.

AI.tldr: Using ALMA observations, the CH₃OH/CH₃CN abundance ratio (~100-200) in the S68N protostellar outflow is found to be nearly constant and can be explained by gas-phase chemistry only with enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates (ζ_CR ~ 10⁻¹⁴ s⁻¹), suggesting this ratio serves as a probe of irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows.
AI.motivation: Chemical correlations between molecules, particularly the CH₃OH/CH₃CN ratio, provide powerful diagnostics to probe the physical conditions and irradiation environment of shocked gas in protostellar outflows.
AI.method: ALMA Band 3 and Band 6 observations of the Class 0 protostar S68N outflow; LTE analysis to derive excitation temperatures and column densities; comparison with up-to-date astrochemical models testing gas-phase CH₃CN formation under varying cosmic-ray ionization rates.
AI.result: Excitation temperatures of 50-60 K; CH₃CN column densities of 2-3×10¹³ cm⁻²; CH₃OH column densities of 3-5×10¹⁵ cm⁻²; CH₃OH/CH₃CN abundance ratio ~100-200, nearly constant along the outflow; reproduced only with ζ_CR up to ~10⁻¹⁴ s⁻¹.
AI.conclusion: The CH₃OH-CH₃CN correlation can be used as a probe of irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows. Further studies should explore grain-surface formation of CH₃CN and extend the analysis to a larger sample.

title: Theoretical determination of the binding energies of methanol and related species onto amorphous solid water ice
comment: Resubmitted to AAS Journals following revision
summary: The formation and survival of complex organic molecules (COMs) in cold interstellar environments depends on their interactions with icy dust grain surfaces. Methanol, a key COM detected in cold cores and protoplanetary disks, is believed to form on amorphous solid water (ASW) through surface reactions and reside there until it is desorbed into the gas phase. We present a theoretical study of the binding energies (BEs) of methanol and its photolysis-derived species on ASW clusters by means of dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT) using a refined protocol implemented in the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP). Molecules capable of hydrogen bonding, such as H2O, CH3OH, HCOOH, and OH, exhibit high BEs and broad BE distributions that reflect the structural heterogeneity of the ASW surface. In contrast, weakly interacting volatiles including CO, CO2, CH4, and CH3 display narrower distributions dominated by dispersion interactions. Open-shell radicals such as CH2OH and OH bind more strongly than HCO and CH3 due to their ability to form directional hydrogen bonds. Incorporation of our BEs into an astrochemical model, in conjunction with a recalculation of the pre-exponential factor using transition state theory, demonstrates the sensitivity of model results to the method of calculation of the grain-surface reaction rates. The new approach generally predicts a higher abundance of radicals on the ice that are key reactants for the formation of COMs when surface diffusion is assumed to be efficient. These findings emphasize the importance of incorporating BEs that have been determined in a self-consistent manner into astrochemical models, and provide reliable theoretical benchmarks for species with limited experimental data.

AI.tldr: This study uses DFT calculations to determine binding energies of methanol and its photolysis-derived species on amorphous solid water clusters, revealing that hydrogen-bonding molecules have high and broad BE distributions while weakly interacting species have narrower distributions, and shows that incorporating these self-consistent BEs into astrochemical models significantly affects predicted radical abundances and COM formation.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and survival of complex organic molecules (COMs) in cold interstellar environments, which depends on their interactions with icy dust grain surfaces, and to provide reliable theoretical benchmarks for binding energies where experimental data is limited.
AI.method: Dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT) using a refined protocol implemented in the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) to compute binding energies of methanol and its photolysis-derived species on amorphous solid water (ASW) clusters.
AI.result: Hydrogen-bonding molecules (H2O, CH3OH, HCOOH, OH) exhibit high BEs and broad distributions reflecting ASW surface heterogeneity; weakly interacting volatiles (CO, CO2, CH4, CH3) show narrower distributions dominated by dispersion; open-shell radicals (CH2OH, OH) bind more strongly than HCO and CH3 due to directional hydrogen bonding; incorporating these BEs into astrochemical models with recalculated pre-exponential factors shows sensitivity to grain-surface reaction rate calculations, generally predicting higher radical abundances on ice when surface diffusion is efficient.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating self-consistently determined binding energies into astrochemical models is important, and this work provides reliable theoretical benchmarks for species with limited experimental data, emphasizing the sensitivity of model results to the method of calculation of grain-surface reaction rates.

title: HI Galaxy Science with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/JingWang01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: This chapter introduces the contributions of the HI galaxy science in this volume reviewing the latest developments and urgent questions in HI galaxy science, providing guiding principles for a layered set of future key science projects. The key science will include: a complete censuses of HI morphologies and kinematics at sub-kpc and 1 km/s resolution within and around galaxies in the nearby Universe; a measurement of the cosmic HI mass density and HI mass function evolution at least up to z~1; an improved understanding of the Universe at z>1, particularly the balance between cold molecular and cool atomic gas. We also provide a view of the synergistic multi-wavelength surveys available in 2028+ in the southern hemisphere. This effort will improve our understanding of the baryon cycle across a significant fraction of the cosmic history, including the processes of gas accretion, consumption and removal as well as AGN and star formation feedback. Based on these science goals, the earlier proposed three-tiered survey strategy remains, but survey parameters and predictions are adjusted according to AA* and AA4 developments. This chapter is an update of the earlier "Advancing Astrophysics with the Square Kilometre Array" chapter 'HI Science with the SKA' by Staveley-Smith & Oosterloo.

AI.tldr: This chapter updates the SKA HI galaxy science roadmap, outlining key science goals including high-resolution HI censuses in the nearby Universe, cosmic HI mass density evolution up to z~1, and cold gas studies at z>1, with a refined three-tiered survey strategy adjusted for AA* and AA4 developments.
AI.motivation: To review the latest developments and urgent questions in HI galaxy science, and provide guiding principles for future key science projects leveraging the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).
AI.method: A layered three-tiered survey strategy (updated from earlier SKA proposals) with parameters adjusted for AA* and AA4 developments, complemented by synergistic multi-wavelength surveys in the southern hemisphere available by 2028+.
AI.result: Key science outcomes include: (1) complete censuses of HI morphologies and kinematics at sub-kpc and 1 km/s resolution in the nearby Universe; (2) measurement of cosmic HI mass density and HI mass function evolution up to z~1; (3) improved understanding of cold molecular vs. cool atomic gas balance at z>1.
AI.conclusion: This effort will improve our understanding of the baryon cycle across cosmic history, covering gas accretion, consumption, removal, and feedback processes from AGN and star formation.

title: Unveiling the roles of thermal and nonthermal processes in the ISM & IGM structure formation and evolution of galaxies with SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2026.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Tabatabaei01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Investigating the thermal and nonthermal processes in the interstellar medium (ISM) and intergalactic medium (IGM) is vital to understanding the evolution of galaxies over cosmic time. Resolved observations with SKA pathfinders show that the nonthermal processes, in which magnetic fields and cosmic rays are involved, can decelerate the formation of massive stars in strongly magnetized regions in nearby galaxies. They can also contribute to the onset of winds and outflows in galaxies. The effects of these processes are stronger at higher redshifts as a result of star formation activities. The SKA Observatory will allow a major breakthrough by mapping the thermal and nonthermal processes in distant universe galaxies, shedding light on the role of the ISM and IGM in the evolution of galaxies. We demonstrate this by simulating the radio continuum and HI emission from local galaxies back to high redshifts. Our simulations show that the AA4 surveys will make it possible to trace the thermal and nonthermal processes of the ISM in galaxies that are analogs to M51 and NGC6946, traced in continuum beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) and the gas content traced by HI beyond z=1. Both simulations and precursor observations indicate the importance of nonthermal feedback at cosmic noon.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates thermal and nonthermal processes (magnetic fields, cosmic rays) in the ISM and IGM, showing via simulations that SKA Observatory surveys (AA4) will enable tracing these processes in distant galaxies beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) for continuum and beyond z=1 for HI, with nonthermal feedback being particularly important at cosmic noon.
AI.motivation: Understanding thermal and nonthermal processes in the ISM and IGM is vital to understanding galaxy evolution over cosmic time, but resolved observations have been limited to nearby galaxies.
AI.method: Simulation of radio continuum and HI emission from local galaxies back to high redshifts, combined with analysis of SKA pathfinder observations and projected AA4 survey capabilities.
AI.result: AA4 surveys will enable tracing thermal and nonthermal ISM processes in M51/NGC6946-analog galaxies beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) in continuum and gas content via HI beyond z=1. Nonthermal feedback is shown to be important at cosmic noon.
AI.conclusion: The SKA Observatory will enable a major breakthrough in mapping thermal and nonthermal processes in distant galaxies, revealing the roles of ISM and IGM in galaxy evolution, with nonthermal feedback playing a key role at cosmic noon.

title: Unveiling a cosmic tango: Integral field spectroscopy and numerical simulations of Arp 143's interaction
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 34 pages, 32 figures
summary: We present spectral data cubes of the interacting galaxy system Arp 143, composed of the ring galaxy NGC 2445 and the lenticular galaxy NGC 2444, obtained with the imaging Fourier transform spectrometer SITELLE at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope. Our data allow to probe the kinematics of the interaction and the chemical properties of the ionized gas. Star-forming regions are almost exclusively found in the ring and nucleus of NGC 2445 with the exception of a few very faint ones discovered at the base of the long tidal plume extending north of NGC 2444. Analysis of the Hα velocity map reveals strong non-circular flows in the ring of NGC 2445, which is expanding. Its nucleus is off-centered with respect to the ring. Oxygen abundance in the ring is on average slightly sub-solar whereas it is close to solar in the nucleus. Broad-band images obtained with the Dragonfly Telephoto array allow to identify the tenuous stellar counterpart of the radio tidal plume. The interaction between the two galaxies is simulated with a chemodynamical evolution code; these simulations suggest that Arp 143 has resulted from a head-on collision between a S0 and a Sc spiral galaxy following a flyby encounter that triggered the formation of the long plume from debris of the disk galaxy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SITELLE spectral data cubes of the interacting galaxy system Arp 143 (ring galaxy NGC 2445 and lenticular NGC 2444), revealing strong non-circular flows in the expanding ring of NGC 2445, sub-solar oxygen abundance in the ring versus solar in the nucleus, and Dragonfly-imaged stellar tidal plume. Chemodynamical simulations suggest Arp 143 formed from a head-on collision between an S0 and a Sc spiral galaxy after a flyby encounter that produced the long plume from disk debris.
AI.motivation: To probe the kinematics and chemical properties of the ionized gas in the interacting galaxy system Arp 143, understand the interaction dynamics, and determine the origin of the ring and tidal plume structures.
AI.method: Imaging Fourier transform spectroscopy (SITELLE at CFHT) for spectral data cubes; Dragonfly Telephoto array for broad-band imaging of stellar counterparts; chemodynamical evolution simulations of the galaxy collision.
AI.result: Star-forming regions are concentrated in the ring and nucleus of NGC 2445 (with a few faint ones at the tidal plume base); Hα velocity map shows strong non-circular, expanding flows in the ring; off-centered nucleus; sub-solar O abundance in ring, solar in nucleus; stellar counterpart of radio tidal plume detected; simulations reproduce a head-on S0-Sc collision from a flyby encounter.
AI.conclusion: Arp 143 is the result of a head-on collision between an S0 galaxy (NGC 2444) and a Sc spiral galaxy (NGC 2445), triggered by a prior flyby that created the long tidal plume from spiral disk debris.

title: Start of orbit librations and the bar growth timescale
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures
summary: We study a dynamical model of the Galaxy with an analytical bar that reproduces the radial velocity $V_R$ profiles as a function of the Galactocentric distance $R$ obtained from the Gaia DR3 data. The model radial velocity profiles show a periodic increase in $V_R$ caused by orbits trapped into libration near the outer Lindblad resonance (OLR). To determine the moment when the librations start, we built a set of additional models differing only in the bar growth time $T_g$. The temporal dependences of the radial velocity $V_R$ in the models with different $T_g$ retain their shape but are shifted relative to each other in time $t$. The shift providing the best agreement between the model dependences is proportional to $T_g$ with the coefficient $k = 0.54 \pm 0.02$. Orbit librations do not start when the bar reaches its full strength, but when it attains only 54% of its maximum strength. Since the maximum bar strength in the models is $Q_b = 0.314$, the librations start when the bar strength reaches $Q_b = 0.170$.

AI.tldr: A dynamical Galaxy model with an analytical bar reproduces Gaia DR3 radial velocity profiles. Orbital librations near the outer Lindblad resonance begin when the bar reaches 54% of its maximum strength (Qb = 0.170), not at full strength.
AI.motivation: To understand the onset conditions of orbital librations near the outer Lindblad resonance in the Milky Way's bar potential, and to link model predictions with observed radial velocity profiles from Gaia DR3.
AI.method: A dynamical model of the Galaxy with an analytical bar was constructed to match Gaia DR3 VR(R) profiles. Multiple models with varying bar growth times Tg were built and compared. The temporal shift between VR(t) curves was measured to determine when librations commence relative to bar growth.
AI.result: The time shift providing best agreement between model dependences is proportional to Tg with coefficient k=0.54±0.02. Orbit librations start when the bar reaches 54% of its maximum strength (Qb = 0.170), not at full strength (Qb = 0.314).
AI.conclusion: Orbital librations near the OLR in the Galaxy initiate at a specific threshold (54% of maximum bar strength), which is critical for understanding the dynamical evolution of the Milky Way and interpreting observed kinematic features.

title: Probing Anomalous Microwave Emission with the Square Kilometre Array
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII(AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Vidal01
summary: Anomalous microwave emission (AME) represents an excess of radiation in the 10-60 GHz range, distinct from synchrotron, free-free, or thermal dust emission. Although most commonly attributed to electric dipole radiation from rapidly rotating small dust grains (spinning dust), alternative mechanisms such as magnetic dipole emission (MDE) remain plausible. The detection of AME across diverse environments, from diffuse interstellar clouds to protoplanetary disks and external galaxies, suggests that multiple physical processes or carriers may contribute to its origin. Understanding AME is essential for both Galactic astrophysics and cosmology, as it constitutes a significant foreground for cosmic microwave background (CMB) studies, potentially biasing measurements. This chapter reviews current theoretical frameworks and observational evidence for AME, highlighting the key outstanding questions concerning its emission mechanisms, carriers, and polarization properties. We discuss how the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), through its unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and frequency coverage, will transform AME studies. SKA observations will enable detailed mapping of AME morphology, precise characterisation of its spectral energy distribution, and the identification of its carriers in Galactic and extragalactic environments. By combining SKA-mid data with higher-frequency observations from ALMA and other facilities such as SPHEREx, it will be possible to disentangle competing models and exploit AME as a diagnostic probe of interstellar grain physics and the small-scale structure of the interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews the current understanding of Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME), an excess radiation in the 10-60 GHz range likely caused by spinning dust grains or magnetic dipole emission. It highlights open questions about AME's mechanisms and carriers, and discusses how the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) will revolutionize AME studies through high sensitivity and resolution, enabling morphological mapping, spectral characterization, and carrier identification, especially when combined with ALMA and SPHEREx.
AI.motivation: AME is a significant foreground for CMB studies and can bias cosmological measurements; understanding its origin is essential for both Galactic astrophysics and cosmology.
AI.method: The chapter reviews theoretical frameworks (spinning dust, magnetic dipole emission) and observational evidence for AME, and discusses how SKAO's sensitivity, resolution, and frequency coverage will enable detailed mapping of AME morphology, spectral energy distribution characterization, and carrier identification, in synergy with ALMA and SPHEREx.
AI.result: AME is detected across diverse environments (diffuse clouds, protoplanetary disks, external galaxies), suggesting multiple physical processes or carriers. Open questions remain about emission mechanisms, carriers, and polarization properties.
AI.conclusion: SKAO will transform AME studies by disentangling competing models and enabling AME to serve as a diagnostic probe of interstellar grain physics and small-scale ISM structure.

title: 3D Magnetic Field Vectors in Space: Bubbles, Clouds, and Filaments
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Tahani01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. 30 pages, 5 figures
summary: Magnetic fields play important roles in the star-formation process across different spatial scales. The interplay between magnetic field strength (a key component of the interstellar medium's energy budget) and field orientation relative to density structures impacts how interstellar material evolves toward star formation. To understand galactic evolution toward stars, planets, and ultimately life, we need to map three-dimensional (3D) magnetic field vectors in 3D space. However, determining full vector information remains challenging due to projection effects and the complex relationship between observable tracers and field geometry. We outline the observational techniques that can be used to probe the 3D magnetic field structures of objects such as supernova remnants (SNR), superbubbles, HII regions, and HI filaments in the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM), and objects in the dense ISM such as molecular clouds, filaments, and cores. The main SKA-specific observational techniques include synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation of both compact sources and the diffuse emission. We discuss how SKA AA4 will allow implementation of the techniques we describe, leveraging the vastly improved sensitivity, resolution and uv-coverage compared to existing datasets. This will enhance our ability to reconstruct 3D magnetic field vectors, advancing our understanding of magnetic fields in Galactic evolution and star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses observational techniques for mapping 3D magnetic field vectors in the interstellar medium using SKA, focusing on synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation to study star-formation processes across different spatial scales.
AI.motivation: Magnetic fields play crucial roles in star formation, but determining full 3D vector information remains challenging due to projection effects and complex relationships between observable tracers and field geometry. The authors aim to outline how SKA can overcome these challenges.
AI.method: The paper outlines observational techniques for probing 3D magnetic field structures, including synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation of both compact sources and diffuse emission, leveraging SKA AA4's improved sensitivity, resolution, and uv-coverage.
AI.result: SKA AA4 will enable vastly improved reconstruction of 3D magnetic field vectors across diverse ISM environments (SNRs, superbubbles, HII regions, HI filaments, molecular clouds, filaments, and cores).
AI.conclusion: Enhanced observational capabilities with SKA AA4 will advance our understanding of magnetic fields' role in Galactic evolution and star formation by enabling better 3D magnetic field vector reconstruction.
